speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The next three years were a battle, which she obviously won, as she was allowed to attend another two years of school before being banished to the upper floor of their house to look after the household and her younger siblings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would imagine how she would sneak books upstairs and hide in dark corners poring through them, as she painstakingly taught herself how to read.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This learning was to be a lifelong journey for her, for even into her 90s, she would carry around a battered old dictionary with her, which she would use to look up words she came across in the newspapers that she did not know.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: She would also marvel at how Singapore's legislative chamber would now comprise 30% women and that there would even be a year officially dedicated to women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But while we applaud the efforts of all that have made progress for women possible, true gender equality is yet to be obtained.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is something that we still have to work towards.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must make sure that the strides that we have taken do not suffer any reversals, as it is indeed threatening to be the case in a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of the issues faced by my grandmother may seem extreme to us with modern eyes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I believe we women still feel the vestiges of such issues, whether it is the promotion or pay raise being held off because we have taken or are about to take maternity leave, or the perception that men should continue to play a secondary role in caring for our loved ones.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I noted that the Government is due to publish its White Paper imminently to review women's issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And the Government has also been carrying out a series of feedback and recommendation sessions through various organisations, ranging from the NTUC Women Committee to the People's Association Women Integration Network, and many more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also noticed that eight days after the notice for this Motion was filed, the PAP Women Wing and Youth Wing released its Joint Paper on Women's Development.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am heartened to see that this flurry of activity indicates that we are not alone in believing that much remains to be done to advance gender equality and to remove barriers to empowering women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Coming back to the reasons for filing this Motion, we at the Workers' Party also believe that it is more important than ever that we talk about the lived experience of our Singaporean women, to identify the areas for improvement and to have a discussion about empowering women to carve out our own roles in Singapore and the world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is why our manifesto for the 2020 General Election contains concrete proposals that address issues relating to improving gender equality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The ideas and topics we will bring up today represents the Workers' Party's contributions to the discussion, based on our own policy proposals, lived experiences and our engagement with fellow Singaporeans and our constituents over the years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is with this in mind that my colleagues and I will today share our thoughts and vision for gender equality in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We believe that it is a good thing that the Government has, over the last 12 months, put in much time and effort into understanding the issues relating to gender equality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This Private Member's Motion is our contribution to this national discourse.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We look forward to seeing the results of the consultations and conversations held, and hope to see substantive legislative action taken to fully enshrine the changes we want to see into law.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, we can and must do more to improve gender equality in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The promise of a society in which every woman and girl enjoys full gender equality, where all legal, social and economic barriers to empowerment have been removed, remains unfulfilled.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When speaking about gender equality, I am often asked – as someone who only has sons – why is this an issue which I feel is important?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why would I want to disadvantage my sons by speaking about empowering women and girls to achieve equality with their male peers?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My answer is simple: gender equality benefits all of society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must stop thinking about gender equality as being gender wars.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially the case in Singapore, where we have been told since a tender age, that our people are our only natural resource.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Women and girls represent half our population, and any form of gender inequality means that we, as a society, are not able to fulfil our full potential.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My sons, along with other boys and men, will and should not be threatened by a more gender equal society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, I believe that they too will benefit when we remove all barriers for both sexes to achieve their full potential and to freely decide whatever role in society each of us chooses to play.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Gender equality should be an aim for all of us and, as we will see during today's debate, men are an integral part of the conversation and must do their part to bring it about.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But before we get carried away slapping ourselves on our back and congratulating ourselves for managing to recruit many allies, we should also pause and ask whether it is helpful to conflate this with the attitude that women need "champions" and "rescuing" by some white knight in shining armour, or if women can be empowered to choose for ourselves the best path forward, noting that my best path may or may not be what the next woman needs or desires.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Of course, we must not forget that there are vulnerable groups of women who do need the protection of the law and wider society, and our suggested approach does not take anything away from that protection.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our concern is when we approach gender equality with preconceived ideas of what is right and wrong for a woman's place in society and how we can help them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not helpful because women are not victims, and to treat us as such only continues to reinforce some of the patriarchal prejudices that have held women back from achieving our fullest potential for too long.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another question we get is why we are focusing so much on this topic while the country is battling a new wave of COVID-19 infections, and there are bigger issues which we need to contend with, instead of opening a debate on gender equality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For us, it does not get any closer to bread and butter issues than this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How to achieve gender equality is a wide topic that comprises many areas, ranging from the gendered impact of ageing, care responsibilities, and our economic and social contributions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleagues and I will today elaborate on each of these and share our thoughts on how we can remove barriers to gender equality, and what support and infrastructure we feel is necessary to better empower women to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the systemic and cultural impediments to gender equality, and what can be done about it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, the adverse effects that the COVID-19 pandemic has brought to women in particular.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, the challenges faced by women as we age.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Starting with the biggest impediment to gender equality, it is our view that if we persist in thinking of "women's issues" and "women's success and progress" through the lens of traditional measures, such as climbing the career ladder and economic earning power, gender equality will be hard to obtain.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Ask parents of young children during lockdown whether they truly understand how essential and difficult the job of teaching and caring for children is, and we would tell you that we do not understand why such crucial labour is generally seen as being low status and is not well paid.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Conversely, the issue cuts both ways: it is a shame that the worth of a man is also often based so much on his ability to earn wages to support his family, with little acknowledgement given to his wish to also participate in the unpaid labour of the household and the care of his loved ones should he choose to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should also strive to respect choices that women make and leave room for women to choose non-conventional paths in life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A woman should not be defined by her relationship status, nor should we judge her for deciding not to have children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of jumping to conclusions and assuming that there must be something wrong if someone, especially a woman, is unmarried or does not have children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps it is time we accept these as one of life's outcomes and move on, instead of constantly questioning what went wrong to lead to it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This approach would also mean much to women – and men – who may be single or childless not by choice, but because of the hand that life has dealt them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this, our media also needs to play its part.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Now that we have laid out the problem, what can we do about it?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There have been many studies that have shown that having enough female leaders is important for any society or organisation to ensure that female perspectives are taken into account, and to give rise to a diversity of views and experiences.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As women, we too need to lead by example in accepting and supporting other women, and to show how this can be done, regardless of the choices we wish to make in life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These range from striving to be corporate or political leaders, to deciding to take time off work to concentrate on starting a family or other interests.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Easily accessible and widely known support and mentorship networks need to be continued to be built up along with formal mentorship programmes, with both female and male mentors, at various levels to support women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Policymakers can help, and should work together with employers and other stakeholders to put in place the right policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, we must remove barriers to women who wish to re-enter the workforce by targeted job-matching and paid re-entry schemes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These schemes could range from mentorships to skills updating and should offer a permanent position at the completion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Participants would benefit from not having to accept a lower pay or a lower-skilled position.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is also a proposal which I spoke on during the 2015 General Election campaign.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also one which the Workers' Party has had in our manifesto since at least 2015.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Beyond this, I am happy to see that there have been calls from all sides for the introduction of anti-discrimination laws to better protect women, especially in the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a crucial yet missing part of our legislative framework.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mandating the obligation of a harassment-free workplace that is imposed on employers sends a strong message to our business community that we, as a society, will not accept discriminatory practices against any of our workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It has been more than 50 years since the Women's Charter was passed in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Likewise, when we consider that not all women tread or should be expected to tread the same path in life, we should consider the aspirations of women and their partners of when and how to start a family.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is why we have, in our last manifesto, a call for the formation of a not-for-profit National Fertility Centre, to provide assisted conception procedures along with advice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More generally, considering the gender angle for any policy being proposed or implemented should also become second nature, and perhaps a national gender scorecard can be created and published in this regard.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This scorecard would track progress – or not, as the case may be – that we have made for matters such as the gender wage gap and contain a regular time use study which quantifies the amount of unpaid work being performed in Singapore on an annual basis, particularly as the bulk of care work is undertaken by women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The scorecard can also profile companies that are leading the way in efforts to increase women's participation in leadership positions and decision-making processes to encourage greater adoption of these best practices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another partner in our quest to change mindsets relating to prejudice and stereotypes would be our schools.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Education is a key way for us to encourage a change in prejudicial mindsets from an early age.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Teachers should be empowered to host frank discussions on gender inequality, the impact of discrimination, and a rethink of gender roles and expectations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An independent review of our school curriculum should also be held, as it can help to propose measures to be applied consistently across all schools to make progress on our gender equality efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to why we need to take action now.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why must we act immediately to put in place the appropriate policies and any legislative amendments while Singapore is still feeling its way out of the pandemic?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It has been found that while men are more likely to suffer ill effects from COVID-19 infections, women across different societies around the world have been disproportionately affected – economically, mentally and physically – by the changes and disruption brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The adverse impact on women stretches across all spheres in a woman's life, from the workplace to the home, as it has been found across all socio-economic classes and societies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On the economic front, women in the labour market have suffered more than men in the economic slump that has followed the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A Politico article published last month cited expert opinions that women in low-wage jobs are most at risk of leaving the workforce permanently, which in turn would have a detrimental effect on our economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A study published in the European Societies journal in September 2020 included women in Singapore in their data and found that across the board, changes in working status to unemployment, reductions in working hours and transitions to working from home have been more frequent for women than for men.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The consequent loss in income or the adverse impact on careers could be irreversible for us who have been so affected.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For women who do manage to hold on to our employment status despite the ever-changing, challenging environment, study after study has found that the transition to alternative working arrangements and the shutting of schools and care support structures have affected women more than men.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Warnings were also sounded that any gains of the last 25 years could be wiped out and there are also many concerns about the impact on the well-being of women who already bear so much mental load of running households.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having myself come through the circuit breaker last year with a very active three- and two-year-old cooped up at home, locking my study door so that I could answer emails and get on Zoom calls while nursing first trimester morning exhaustion and morning sickness, with our usual main support network in my parents cut off, I often wonder how I managed to survive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I know that I only managed to juggle my full-time job due to an extremely understanding boss.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I can only imagine how much worse this would have been for other women such as single mothers and families who do not have access to help at home or a support network.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These challenges are further exacerbated by how gender-based violence too has increased since the beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These developments are worrying and tell us that addressing gender equality must be done even as we continue to tackle the effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The fragility of progress in gender equality itself is also a matter for consideration as we build further policies to ensure that future shocks to society do not result in such reversals in the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleagues will continue to set out our proposals to address this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is ageing and by 2030, 25% of our population is expected to be aged 65 and above.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means that more Singaporeans would need help to perform day-to-day tasks and will cease to be active members of the workforce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is, therefore, essential that we put in place sustainable policies to address these concerns.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a first step, we repeat our previous call for better recognition of those who carry out these informal caring responsibilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is only by measuring the contributions of unpaid workers and publishing it as a supplement to our GDP data that we can start developing policies to guard against these workers, who tend to be overwhelmingly female, from becoming destitute in what should be their golden years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To add to the challenges women face, the life expectancy at birth in 2020 for women was 86.1, compared with 81.5 for men.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, women are more likely to take on a disproportionate role in providing informal care, be it for their children, husbands or elders, often at an economic cost as we often have to scale back on the type or amount of paid employment taken on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Coupled with the gender wage gap, this is something that has serious implications on women's financial resources and, in particular, retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, the various top-up schemes available have not addressed this gap between the genders, hence our call to relax rules on the transfer of CPF funds before the age of 55 after the Minimum Sum has been met, to allow transfers to older relatives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I note there are more top-up schemes available now, it is not yet clear what the impact is on women's retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to continue to question gender norms that view informal caring as primarily a job for women, and instead encourage a more equal distribution of such responsibilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the problem will, of course, not be solved overnight.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, it is also key that women who currently shoulder the responsibilities of informal care do not end up being further penalised by our policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, the Workers' Party has spoken up against the Government's current policy of requiring higher CareShield Life premiums to be paid by women as this, at best, causes a double penalty on many women who are already struggling with a gender wage gap and taking on less paid work due to their caring responsibilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Creating this heavier burden on women, therefore, does not move us in the right direction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, yes, we can be proud of the progress that we have made for gender equality so far.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But as has already been acknowledged by many in this House, much work needs to be done.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should not get so carried away by our perceived successes and with patting ourselves on our backs that we miss this key moment to effect sustainable change for gender equality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have outlined some of the key areas of concern in this speech and my colleagues in the Workers' Party will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also believe that all of us here do want to ensure that we work together to engender a whole-of-society effort to empower every woman to freely realise her full potential and participation in society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In that spirit, I look forward to a collegial, frank and honest debate on the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The choice of words in today's Motion, led by my Parliamentary colleague Ms He Ting Ru, is significant and deliberate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Motion refers to each woman freely realising her full potential and participation in society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The word "freely" refers to how different women may choose different pathways at different stages in their lives, without facing significant disadvantages for the decisions they make.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why does our Motion speak of the need to strive for gender equality?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Because obstacles bar the way to that today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These obstacles lie in our ecosystem of laws and regulations, which present challenges in terms of discrimination in the workplace and insurance premiums, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Parliamentary colleagues and I from the Workers' Party will cite more examples and offer proposals to address these.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These obstacles also lie in cultural norms, the unspoken assumption that a woman should bear more of the burden of housework even if she has a career like her husband; or the assumption that the mother has to be the one responsible for the child’s academic progress in school and liaising with teachers more than the father.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The obstacles to gender equality also lie in our minds; in the mind of the woman who hesitates to speak up at company meetings such that her male colleagues hog the air-time; or in the mind of the man who believes he can sexually harass a female co-worker with impunity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In debating this important Motion, let us address ourselves to these three types of impediments to full gender equality: the structural, the cultural and the psychological.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All of society will gain if we succeed in that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Because every woman freely realising her full potential will mean that every woman can give of her best in the workplace and in the home, assured of an environment where she is given opportunities and support that are not less than any man.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It means that every woman can strive for new heights in her professional field and contribute fully to leadership.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would mean a better, stronger society, which benefits men too.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The obstacles outlined above underscore the need for us to review the challenges facing the diversity of roles women take on in society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For this speech, Madam, I will take reference from the three most important women in my life: my wife, my mother and my daughter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is with that reference that I shall touch on three segments of women today: the homemaker, the career women and the young woman who is our hope for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In today’s world and with Singapore’s high cost of living, the decision to be a homemaker is not made lightly by either wife or husband.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My wife was an executive in the fields of public service, communications and academic administration before becoming a full-time homemaker, transitioning via a period of flexible working.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Her day is packed as she makes many decisions, while providing a great deal of parenting attention to our teenage children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In my wife’s case, she sacrificed a dynamic professional career in the media industry for the sake of focusing on our two young children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many women make this choice knowing that they would have enjoyed more lucrative outcomes if they had stayed on in their careers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some women who make this choice find themselves struggling economically in later life, as Ms He Ting Ru referred to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many women outlive their husbands – life expectancies being what they are – and many have insufficient funds in their CPF, or an insufficient inheritance from their late husbands or support from their children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But this is still a drop in the ocean and does not fully address the problem, if you consider the numbers of women who find themselves in this position.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can quantifying the economic contribution that a homemaker makes help us design policy solutions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An ILO study from 2018 of 60 countries found that men spend 83 minutes a day on unpaid household work whereas women spend three times that, at 265 minutes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Academic studies have been conducted to attempt to quantify the commercial value of the work a homemaker does in other countries, yielding various dollar figures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not fair that women who sacrifice to build a home and support their children should have to struggle later in life because of an inequitable sharing of family earnings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, many women who become homemakers would like to have the choice of going into part-time, flexible work or job sharing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Employers should strive to make more of such options available, as many more progressive employers already do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim will speak more on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather than focusing on consulting work for companies to create more flexible work arrangements, rather than supporting that in Government schemes as a focus, I would urge the Government to consider more schemes that directly financially support, during the transition period, mothers and fathers who want to transition from a homemaker role to part-time work, nudging people to make such a choice and, thus, helping to use local talent to boost our Labour Force Participation Rate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As the largest employer, the Public Service should set an example here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2016, I asked a Parliamentary Question on job sharing and flexible work in the Public Service, revealing that there were 2,000 public officers on part-time arrangements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If the Public Service takes a proactive approach to designing and offering part-time jobs or job sharing rather than only reactively considering applications for such from their full-time officers, it could well find that it is able to tap on a broader field of talent, as well as help ex-officers transition back to full-time work at their own pace.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, many homemakers these days are experimenting with becoming home-based entrepreneurs, working flexibly and often using digital platforms like YouTube videos, virtual meeting providers and e-commerce enabling platforms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope that such home-based entrepreneurs can obtain the same access to startup grants as other kinds of startups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would urge our social enterprises and trade associations and chambers to support such micro-entrepreneurship and publicise good case studies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Supporting home-based micro-businesses enriches the ecosystem of options that women, and, indeed, men, have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I think back to my wife, I would want her to live in a society which respects and recognises the work she does and gives her many meaningful choices for her future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My lodestar when I think about working women is my own mother, who was an excellent, recognised Primary school teacher in a neighbourhood school, and who held up more than her fair share of the work at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many women, like my mother did, toil in the workplace and also, bear an unequal share of housework and parenting work at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many also face a non-level playing field at work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, surveys show that perceptions of discrimination are not small.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This 15% figure does not seem to me to gel with only 400 discrimination cases a year and only 13% of that 400 leading to actual findings of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There could be under-reporting by those who have concerns, by those who feel that they may be on the receiving end of discrimination but have concerns about confidentiality, or are unclear about what is discrimination, or are pessimistic of the odds of success.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, some of my constituents have shared such concerns with the current discrimination complaints handling regime.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently, from my experience, there is a perception also on the other side among firms, employers, that TAFEP guidelines are not sufficiently clear as to what constitutes a breach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is also a perception among potential complainants that the burden of proof is on them and the odds of success are not high, which the 13% figure seems to be consistent with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, the prospect of an offence by a company would have a stronger deterrent effect than that of merely being found in breach of non-mandatory guidelines and, if you are in the 13%, merely being subject to curtailment of work pass privileges, which is not a publicly known demerit, as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, not every company would be equally dependent on foreign work passes, so that lever of control would have variable efficacy and deterrent effects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is an argument, Madam, that anti-discrimination laws would deter investment into Singapore and be anti-business.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, many companies would benefit from the greater clarity and stronger penalties that such laws provide, as it would enable them to pressure their middle managers more effectively to stop discriminatory practices and, thus, protect their companies from reputational risk, like if an ex-employee takes to social media to allege discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 2007 UNESCO study found that much talent is being wasted as women turn away from science and technology careers as a result of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A World Bank study also found that gender gaps in education and employment considerably reduce economic growth in countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We in the Workers’ Party welcome this change and look forward to the outcome of this review.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is more that companies can do to level the playing field for working women.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, promoting shared paternity and maternity leave, another Workers’ Party manifesto point which my colleague Mr Louis Chua will expand on; countering sexual harassment in the workplace which my colleague Ms Raeesah Khan will speak on; and making available pump rooms and enabling parents to bring children to work under certain circumstances, where practicable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is important for us to remember what is at stake in ensuring a level playing field for women.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A fairer workplace will bring more women into the workforce and enhance our labour force participation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, giving women a fair deal in the workplace is not just about the workplace.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is about ensuring that women have a fair deal at home and across society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Which brings me to the third and last part of my speech, on young women and how we bring about a change in culture and mindsets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I speak passionately about this because I am thinking about my daughter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She is the only extrovert in the family.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She has far more friends than I had at her age, maybe even at my age right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have raised her to choose her own path freely and to never feel less than anyone else because of her gender or the colour of her skin; and I am proud that she lives and breathes those values.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It has to be rooted in our culture and our mindsets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Too many men, and even women, still feel that the man should be the dominant partner at home; that men have the right to dominate the air-time and the rewards at work; and that "men will be men" socially and standing up to sexual harassment is futile, or worse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What we need is a culture where men, and women, openly acknowledge and shift social mores against non-gender-neutral policies, practices, behaviours and assumptions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I would like to speak about men.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Men need to reflect on our own mindset towards gender equality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: From my experience, I do not believe that most men want their wives, mothers, daughters and female friends to live in a gender-unequal society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Having said that, some men continue to harbour sexist attitudes when it comes to things like the notion of consent and when it comes to parenting and housekeeping at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to continue to shine the light on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Whole-of-society efforts – from Government, business, NGOs and ordinary citizens – are needed to banish these attitudes into the rubbish bin of history.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We cannot adopt the dangerous assumption that these anachronistic attitudes will naturally disappear over time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I made a similar argument when speaking on the Aspirations of Singapore Women Motion in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to address the concerns of some men who have opined that too much talk about sexism against women is in itself sexist and equivalent to misandry or the hatred of men.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I had to look this word up, and I do not know if I am pronouncing it correctly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The argument used here is that men are placed at a disadvantage due to having to serve National Service and Reservist duty and due to the effect of the Women's Charter on events like divorce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not disagree that there are men who need help and may face unequal treatment in certain contexts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some men experience abuse from the women in their lives or, as stay-at-home fathers, may face difficulties collecting maintenance payments, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many men struggle to balance Reservist obligations with the demands of their career.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I would urge men to reflect on the fact that while there has been progress, sexism and gender inequality also harm men.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Diminished opportunities or discrimination at work against women mean that men have to step up and bear more of the income-earning burden in the household.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Sexist expectations in the workplace and at home can deprive men of the opportunity to be equal co-parents with their wives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Gender stereotypes also hurt men, for example, the social stigma against men who earn less, who are caregivers and who make non-mainstream career choices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, women still face unequal challenges on the whole.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Bridging the gap on these issues help the mother, daughters and wife of every man.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A shift in the perception of these issues would also signal to men that they have the freedom not to conform to existing stereotypes and expectations placed on them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, remedying these issues is, ultimately, in the interest of every man.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My wife and I are doing our best to raise our 13-year-old son to deeply internalise these values.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The progress he has made thus far gives me cause for pride.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When we think of engineers and scientists, will we be gender-blind?

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Participants include men and women, young and old, homemakers, professionals, executives, social workers, students and many more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And they have provided many suggestions and feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Women organisations such as the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO), NTUC Women and Family Unit and the People's Association (PA) Women's Integration Network hosted many of these conversations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Other women organisations including PAP Women's Wing, AWARE, trade association women sub-groups and student union groups have submitted their recommendations before the stipulated deadline of 31 July 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government had said at the onset of the Conversations that it would consolidate views from the conversations and present action plans for the future in the form of a White Paper.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The White Paper would form the basis for a full debate in Parliament as it would have taken the range of views expressed by all participants throughout the process into account.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For today, I will focus on the historical context for women's development in Singapore and also provide an update on the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We cannot look at issues in silos, at a point in time, without understanding where they sit, relative to the bigger picture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The past 130 years has been a time of great awakening and great progress for women in many parts of the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Women's suffrage gained momentum in the early 1900s in the Western world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: From the 1930s, there were more jobs for women in the developed world as the services industry grew.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore found itself in these worldwide winds of change as we moved towards Independence in the 1950s.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But what was the status of our women then and what path did we set ourselves on?

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The early PAP party leaders had a vision for the women of Singapore and they believed in women's advancement and gender equality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I have with me the original copy of the People's Action Party's (PAP) manifesto for the Legislative Assembly Elections in 1959.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under its proposed programme, item 10 states: "To raise the status of women by introducing a monogamous marriage law".

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This was further elaborated in the PAP's five-year plan for 1959 to1964 titled "The Tasks Ahead" where there is a specific section on the emancipation of women and I read: "Women who form nearly half of our population have an important part to play in our national construction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the first instance, in order to emancipate them from the bonds of feudalism and conservatism, a monogamous marriage law will be passed." Further down in the paragraph, "We shall foster the principle, if necessary by legislation, that there shall be equality of women with men in all spheres and we shall encourage them to come forward to play a leading role in politics, administration, business and industry, education and in other spheres." Faithful to its publicly declared goals, the PAP took action when it formed the Government in 1959.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is most apt then, that 60 years later, in September 2020, to advance the trajectory of women's progress and to provide them with enhanced protection, that our current Minister for Law, Mr K Shanmugam, would initiate the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is the PAP Government's continued commitment to the advancement of our Singapore women, in partnership with the whole of society, to continue to support, enable and empower our women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Between the passing of the Women's Charter in 1961 till today, Singapore underwent rapid transformation and the status of women improved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The political leaders rightly reasoned that for Singapore to be lifted from its fairly low economic status in the 1950s, it needed its entire population to be as highly educated and economically productive as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Singapore Government systematically introduced and improved legislation, policies and initiatives to advance the progress of Singapore women and worked in close partnership with the community over the years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Forty-one ruling party women Members of Parliament, seven Opposition women Members of Parliament and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, and 34 female Nominated Members of Parliament have sat in this House to vote on legislation which empowers our women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First on the agenda was the need to make quality education freely accessible to both boys and girls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Universal education for children of all races, gender and backgrounds was implemented.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Boys and girls were equally valued and given as much opportunity as possible to pursue education and skills-based training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The female share of University intake has remained at about 50% since around 1980.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Healthcare services for women and girls were improved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Did you know that in 1966, KK Women's and Children's Hospital entered the world records for delivering the highest number of newborns within a single medical facility for that year and continued to hold the record for the next 10 years?

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And we continue to care for the physical and mental well-being of our women and girls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: My colleague, Ms Rahayu Mahzam, will touch on this later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Female labour force participation rate for those aged 15 and above went up from around 21.6% in 1957, to 29.5% in 1970.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Current programmes such as Career Trial and Jobs Growth Incentive also encourage women who have left the workforce to re-enter the workforce, and tripartite partners work with employers to promote pro-family work environments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The community had also been active to promote women's advancement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the 1970s to 1980s, several women's organisations such as SCWO, NTUC Women's Committee, PAP Women's Wing, AWARE and AWWA were formed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 1978, the first Family Service Centre opened to support vulnerable women and families in need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 1996, the National Family Violence Networking System, which involved various community partners, was set up to address the problem of family violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government also knew that women needed to be supported as they strived to balance caregiving and work-life harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 2001, the first Marriage and Parenthood Package was launched, followed by subsequent Packages in 2004, 2008 and beyond.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Leave provisions for mothers and fathers were increased over the years and additional support was provided for families via subsidies for maternity-related medical costs and other expenses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Separately, subsidies for childcare and infant care were also provided to families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As Singapore went from mudflats to metropolis, the Singapore women similarly made significant strides over the years and their contributions are integral to our Singapore story.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And I hope that the Members who have spoken before me would be pleased to note that many of their inputs have been reflected in the key themes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We heard Singaporeans' aspirations and hopes for Singapore women: (a) that women and men are equally empowered to achieve their career aspirations, and women would not be denied opportunities on the basis of gender and/or family commitments; (b) that caregivers' contributions to society are better recognised, and there is more sharing of caregiving responsibilities between men and women; (c) that stronger protection will be provided to women; (d) that support be strengthened for vulnerable groups of women; (e) undergirding these aspirations, participants hoped that we could overcome traditional mindsets and stereotypes about gender roles in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: My colleagues and I were greatly inspired by participants' vision of a Singapore where women and men work as close partners so that real choices are enabled for women, and where whole of society works together, so that everyone can achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We thank everyone for participating actively and for sharing your personal stories, challenges, aspirations and ideas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While the 31 July deadline for submission of feedback has passed, we understand that many Singaporeans and local organisations are still brimming with ideas for Singapore women's progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Any new ideas from today's session will also feed into the overall process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We continue to welcome your feedback, so please send them to us before end-August.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Even as we are reviewing the feedback and preparing the White Paper for debate in Parliament, we have begun work to address some of the feedback that we have received, building on what we have already been doing to support Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The inter-agency Task Force on Family Violence will release its recommendations later this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MCI launched a Singapore Together Alliance for Action to tackle online harms, especially those targeted at women and girls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To cultivate a shift in mindsets, MOE has enhanced its Character and Citizenship Education curriculum to build an appreciation of the equity of roles in the family, respect for both genders and the importance of not ascribing to gender stereotypes when considering education and career pathways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To review how we can stamp out discrimination in the workplace, MOM announced that it was setting up a tripartite committee to study whether legislation should be pursued and its appropriate scope.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If you want to go far, go together." In the past 60 years, we have made significant progress because of partnership at all levels of society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This year, through the Conversations launched by the Government, we will have outlined and united around a common vision for Singapore women's progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Individuals, families, employers and the community have all played important roles in this partnership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the next lap of our journey, let us all work even more closely together, towards a fairer and more inclusive society where our Singapore women can realise their fullest potential.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   In the past 50 years, the status of Singapore women has improved significantly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The female labour force participation rate has risen steadily, about half of Singapore’s University graduates each year are women, and Singapore consistently ranks amongst the top internationally on indices related to women’s development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The development of Singapore women has benefited from economic development, social progress and the tireless efforts of the PAP Government over the years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 1961, the Women's Charter, which was spearheaded by Ms Chan Choy Siong and others from the PAP, came into effect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This was a major breakthrough at the time and signalled a big step forward for Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Charter legislates monogamy, emancipating women from the bonds of feudalism and conservatism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It also protects the rights of women in marriage and divorce, provides for the maintenance of wives and children, and punishes crimes against women and girls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Since then, the PAP Government has remained steadfast in its commitment to further the advancement of women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This includes improving childcare and healthcare services, prioritising the development of children, making universal education available, promoting equality between women and men, encouraging women to pursue higher education, protecting workers' rights and encouraging women to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our efforts paid off and together we went through the changes of times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In order to provide care for women of all ages, the Government has introduced a series of policies to address their different needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, older women may worry about not having enough retirement funds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They worry about what happens if they fall ill or if their husband falls ill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, the Government has also introduced the Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation packages to reduce the burden of medical expenses for the elderly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In 2019, MOH also introduced the Caregiver Support Action Plan to strengthen support for caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For the new generation of Singaporean women, they want to pursue their dreams and hope that they can take good care of their families and children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the one hand, the Government provides equal education opportunities for women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Schools now have an Education and Career Guidance programme to encourage girls to choose science, engineering, mathematics and other courses to facilitate their participation in a wider range of industries in future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the other hand, the Government has been investing heavily in early childhood education and infant care services in recent years, to reassure mothers and provide children with accessible, affordable and quality education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, we have been listening closely to women’s voices and the community’s feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In September last year, the Government launched the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development to better understand the current development of women and their concerns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I am glad to note that the participants have responded enthusiastically and shared their ideas and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also collect any new suggestions from Members of Parliament today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We look forward to more in-depth discussion on women’s issues, to provide solutions to outline a common vision for the advancement of Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The PAP Government has always been a strong advocate of women's development, in the past and at present.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Looking ahead, we will continue to work tirelessly for the development of Singapore women, with community partners and organisations, building on the hard work of our predecessors.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My speech today will touch on the unequal distribution of care responsibilities and how this is linked to discriminatory social institutions and stereotypes about gender roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The changes in working patterns due to the COVID-19 pandemic have increased the spotlight on gender inequality that exists at home and, in particular, the difficulties women face in being both caregivers and breadwinners.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Strong societal recognition of shared responsibilities helps reduce the disadvantages women face in the workplace, including the "motherhood penalty", "mom guilt" and stigma that they face when they want to return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Women would have more time for themselves to rest, to pursue their aspirations freely and to contribute even more to the community at large.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, men too will be able to put aside their fears of being discriminated against at the workplace, facing backlash for their lack of perceived work commitment, in trying to take on greater responsibility for caregiving roles at home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Sad to say, we are not quite there yet and the idea of equal, shared responsibilities remains an ideal.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this year, I recall watching a documentary series produced by CNA, "Give Mum A Break!", which documents three Singaporean households and what happens at home when moms are shipped off to a four-day, three-night staycation, leaving dads to hold the fort at home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They struggled, to say the least, and while it was amusing to watch, truth be told, I have doubts in my mind whether I can survive being at home on a one-to-one basis with my two-year-old toddler and for three nights straight.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need not look further than Singapore's official manpower statistics to see such effects play out.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Of the men reported to be outside the labour force, a mere 0.2% cited housework as the main reason for not working, which is the least common reason among men.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is in stark contrast for women where housework was the most common reason for not working, coming in at 21.5% of women outside the labour force.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this survey was from 2013, this reinforces the societal standards that have been placed on women to take on the larger responsibility in their households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Statistics aside, few would disagree that much of today's unpaid care work is still done by women as it is largely considered a female responsibility.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there is an increased awareness of shared responsibility within and between households today, there is much work that remains invisible and unpaid.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This needs to be urgently addressed if we are to advance women's development in Singapore because such work, if it remains unpaid and unnoticed, has effects on the female labour force participation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Recognising unpaid labour, whether carried out by men or women, must, therefore, be the first step in addressing the disadvantages faced by those that take on the bulk of unpaid labour for a household.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There should be annual measures of the amount of unpaid work undertaken by Singaporeans and this should be published as a supplement to national GDP data, as shared by my colleague, Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An International Labour Organization report published in 2018 estimated that women in APEC countries do four times more unpaid care work than men.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the local context, the study by Ipsos and UWS I referred to earlier highlighted that women are doing more unpaid domestic work than men think they are.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The study notes that while gender-defined roles still exist in the Singaporean household and are held by both men and women, the younger generation holds these views less.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Society is moving towards acceptance and being supportive of equal caring responsibilities and this is encouraging.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But we can do more as we create our roadmap towards gender equality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is often suggested that to address the unequal distribution of caring responsibilities, we must begin by addressing internalised gender norms and stereotypes in redistributing responsibilities for care and housework between women and men.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In today's context, we need to be mindful that gender norms and stereotypes may be internalised differently for different groups.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As suggested by AWARE, a review should be conducted via an intersectional lens to understand the differential impact it has on not just men and women, but those with disabilities, ethnic minority women, migrant women and so on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a starting point, as lawmakers, it is important for us to do a stock-take on our existing policies, to ensure that our care-related policies do not ironically perpetuate stereotypes and reinforce notions on gender roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, we need to provide adequate support to all caregivers in Singapore to enable all caregivers, whether women or men, to freely realise their full potential in society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My fellow Sengkang Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has asked about instituting different tiers of childcare leave such that those with more children will be entitled to comparatively more days of leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my MOM Committee of Supply (COS) speech earlier this year, I too called for childcare leave to be extended on a per child basis and up to the age of 12, as our Primary school-going children would still need a degree of care if they fell ill, or simply to allow families to spend more time together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic over the last one and a half years has also compounded the problem, where a Stay-Home Notice issued to children who are down with respiratory symptoms would effectively wipe out five days of leave for working parents, making it extremely challenging for parents to balance their work commitments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many companies have started to offer eldercare leave as an Employee Value Proposition and I have asked if this could be considered as statutory leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO) has advocated to make childcare leave and eldercare leave interchangeable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: AWARE too has suggested that the Government could implement the statutory right to request for flexible work arrangements, as well as making paid eldercare leave and family care leave mandatory for sandwiched caregivers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, the Singapore Alliance for Women in Ageing (SAWA) has called for the conversion of childcare leave to family care leave, which could allow other members of the family to help provide the necessary care for persons who need it.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are worthy suggestions to improve the ecosystem of support for women caregivers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, changing family structures require more flexible guidelines for support, such as expanding the definitions of leave and subsidies, to ensure that all caregivers are supported.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, extended families providing care on a regular basis for children of our frontline workers during this pandemic, or grandparents who provide care to the grandchildren, whom the MOH recognises as essential and would not be counted towards the prevailing permissible visitor cap per household, or to the number of social gatherings per day.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These caregivers are currently not entitled to caregiving or childcare leave, unlike their peers who have children.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The reality is, caregiving responsibilities between parents of children go beyond the couple.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It takes a village to raise a child and our policies should provide new recognition to the village and to go beyond merely adopting a so-called "practical approach to calibrating childcare leave provisions".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, despite the release of the Tripartite Standard on Flexible Work Arrangements in 2017, true flexible work arrangements only became commonplace in Singapore due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, FWAs come in a spectrum and, clearly, the level of flexibility that was in place pre-COVID-19 is dramatically different from what we have seen in 2020, or even today with Work-from-Home being the default work arrangement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Calling on employers to implement good practices and foster more family-friendly work environments may not be enough, particularly when much of caregiving right now is narrowly defined as childcare, care for disabled persons or for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Caregiving should be as broad, gender-neutral and norm-free as possible if we are to ensure greater equality for women in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we do not address unequal care responsibilities, caring can become a drain on Singapore's workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Caring tends to be overlooked in the workplace, leading to some having to choose between gainful employment and their families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the near future, this could apply not only to women, but to men as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is pertinent because with life expectancy increasing and slower population growth, we must begin to make changes so that employers can better support workers that have work and care responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One way is to ensure that managers are adequately trained to overcome unconscious gender-bias towards employees.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This should be a mandatory part of workplace training if workplaces are to become more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Male-dominated industries should also review their diversity policy and enhance support in the workplace, including recognising men as caregivers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, men are also sons, fathers, brothers and more.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Men may be concerned about being discriminated against professionally, missing out on promotions and pay increases, marginalised, or even laughed at for taking time off.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Gender norms and stereotypes are also damaging for men, and while cultural and mindset shifts are important, institutional changes are also going to be necessary if we are to move towards equal care responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my next point on the role of fathers in a child's development.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a father to a two-year-old toddler, I am thankful to have witnessed his various development milestones over the past two years, and partake in the joys of parenthood, while continuing to stay productive at work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Psychological research across families from different ethnic backgrounds suggests that fathers' affection and increased family involvement help promote children's social and emotional development.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, according to research by Dads for Life, there has been a continued lag in terms of fathers' involvement compared to mothers, in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some of these, as discussed earlier, is due to entrenched gender norms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Teachers may call up the child's mothers instead of their fathers, as fathers may be perceived as "too busy working".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A Dads for Life Fatherhood Perception Survey in 2010 highlighted that 39% of fathers surveyed said that society's views on how men should behave also posed challenges to them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There must be more attention given to fatherhood and to the diverse range of fathering practices and for further local research to understand and support fathers' involvement as the times change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should not blame women's education and careers leading to calls for more equal parenting, and instead be channelling more time and effort to understanding and overcoming the challenges men's roles in care-giving, including fatherhood.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The last Fatherhood Perception Survey was done more than 10 years ago and is long overdue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What can we do as lawmakers to make this change?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is where our existing care-related policies covering Government-paid maternity and paternity leave run the danger of further reinforcing gender roles and stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When my son was born, as much as I would like to be alongside my wife on our parenthood journey as first-time parents, the mere two weeks of paternity leave was not even sufficient to last throughout my wife's confinement period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would encourage closer parental bonds with children while having positive effects on the relationship between the parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Shared parental leave supports fathers who want to partake in the joys of parenthood and allows them the flexibility to take on greater responsibilities in childcare to support their wives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, the Workers' Party also shared in our manifesto the need to increase the number of infant care centres to better serve the needs of young families and the motivation behind this is manifold.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having adequate infant and childcare places will allow caregivers, both men and women, to free up some of their time in the day and play the necessary roles of a parent, employee and individual, without having to sacrifice their career or retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As such, while there may be vacancies in the system as a whole today, this may not be so for particular areas with a higher concentration of young families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, the Workers' Party also called for childcare subsidies to be equalised for all children, regardless of the employment status of their mothers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At present, mothers of Singaporean children working at least 56 hours a month are entitled to additional childcare subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This, however, does not take into account the unpaid care or voluntary work that other mothers take on, or those who are engaged in part-time work due to their care commitments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All these, ultimately, shows the importance of state policies in enabling women, and men, who are key members of our families and society, to be supported in their efforts as a parent, individual and employee.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Building strong families and societies must start with supporting parents with young children to achieve their fullest potential, all whilst becoming a more involved parent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Post-pandemic, companies should consider making flexible work arrangements a norm at workplaces, as many forward-thinking companies have already done so to boost employee productivity and promote talent retention.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As individuals, we should not be afraid to challenge archaic gender stereotypes and to support our own families to the best of our abilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, more importantly, as lawmakers today, we have an opportunity to set the right tone on gender equality in Singapore and it is imperative for the Government to demonstrate leadership on this matter by setting right our current care-related policies today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even in developed countries like the UK and the US, women obtained only basic legal rights such as the right to vote in 1918 and 1919 respectively, thanks to the efforts of early women's rights activists like the suffragettes, the century before that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
