text: Around the 1960s and 1970s, women's movements started taking off again in the Western world as the movement focused on political and economic rights, and substantive equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Helen Reddy's famous song, "I am woman" was from this era, in 1971, topping the charts in 1972.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, we can imagine some of the issues that were present at that time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Consent of the married couple was also made a requirement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Rights and duties of husbands were legislated for and protections were put in place in the event marriages broke down.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This legislation was ground-breaking at the time, forcing many established practices to change.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Since then, women have made leaps and strides in the journey to equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have seen this in my own family.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both my grandmothers had their education cut short in Primary school as a result of World War II.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One was told that being too educated would make it more difficult to get married.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The other, who was the eldest child in her family, had lost her own mother and had to take care of her younger siblings, so she took on a caregiving role as a young teenager.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Their children, my parents' generation, were born during the post-war baby boom.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The daughters of that generation, unlike their mothers, had the opportunity to attend and complete school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, Primary school was mandatory for many of them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My maternal grandmother, who was an excellent cook, refused to allow any of her four daughters to assist in the kitchen, insisting they study instead.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This generation of women who joined the workforce in the 1970s and 1980s were more economically independent than the generation before them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This period also saw women become global leaders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Leaders of this era included Golda Meir in Israel, Margaret Thatcher in the UK, Indira Gandhi in India and Benazir Bhutto in Pakistan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was quite clear that women were capable of leadership at the highest levels.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my household, my father and mother both supported each other in caregiving and providing, and they also had support from our grandparents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In contrast to my mother who was kept out of the kitchen by her own mother, my mother actually got me my very first cookbook back when I was in Primary school and encouraged me to try out the recipes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When my mother went off to further her studies for three years while my brother and I were in Primary school, my father and his parents played the main caregiving role.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Essentially, I grew up without too many stereotypes on male and female roles and believing that women could do and achieve anything men could and, likewise, that men could also play a part in the household.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Primary school, I was fortunate to be in the top class in my Primary school, but boys were outnumbered by girls, two to one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I went to an all-boys Secondary school, but in Junior College, again I was outnumbered in class, boys to girls, two to one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In University, all around me, women were very well represented and the law faculty had around equal numbers of men and women.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, after entering the workforce and starting my own family, I realised that women still face obstacles to attaining substantive equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are not as many women as men in leadership positions in organisations and women still end up being the primary caregivers for children and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Usually, because they are the primary caregivers, they will drop out of the workforce or work part-time at some stage of their working lives, which in turn feeds into more difficulties getting back into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These issues are often more difficult to solve as they involve changing not just laws but social attitudes and "invisible" barriers or "glass" ceilings.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These have been matters that the Government has continued to focus on over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I attended one of these dialogues, along with Minister Indranee Rajah with Indian and Sikh women, organised by SINDA, REACH and the Young Sikh Association.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   In this dialogue with Indian women that Ms Indranee Rajah and I participated in, we broke up into smaller groups, each focused on different issues women face in achieving equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One set of issues raised by women was that although the laws were in place for equality, family and societal expectations had not changed to a large extent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One woman, who was a scientist in her 30s, mentioned that her family members still keep pressurising her about marriage.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: She also mentioned that many of the men she meets are intimidated when they find out she has a PhD and is engaged in research.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A number of women echoed issues related to discrimination at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The law is clear that pregnant women cannot be discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, some women indicated that notwithstanding this, employers sometimes express displeasure when a woman is pregnant, especially in the case of smaller companies, which puts them under pressure with bosses and colleagues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Senior care leave is not provided for and senior activity and daycare centres are not as readily accessible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also a tremendous emotional burden when caring for loved ones in their twilight years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Divorce also carried stigma and some continued to remain in abusive marriages because of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Despite all the issues raised though, almost all the women acknowledged that tremendous strides have been made in relation to women's issues in the course of their lifetimes and almost all had better opportunities than their mothers and grandmothers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The journey to get more equal outcomes for women is ongoing and one that our Government has been pushing hard since Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the Motion rightly acknowledges, this is a whole-of-society effort to remove the barriers, both visible and invisible, to help women achieve their full potential.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would, however, like to go a little further and would like to see action and concrete steps to help remove these barriers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many conversations with different groups of women had been taking place, similar to the one I had mentioned earlier, and I expect there will be interesting insights from these Conversations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What I hope is that the findings in these dialogues can be converted to action plans.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of the amendment?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Yes, I have given copies to the Clerks for distribution.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Right, we will distribute the amendment to the Members.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Motion as proposed by the Workers' Party is one that I think everyone in this House agrees with and as my colleague, Ms Sun Xueling set out, has been in line with the Government's efforts since inception and over the last year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I propose that the debate of this amendment take place concurrently with the debate on the main topic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I look forward to support for this amendment from my colleagues in the Workers' Party too.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: The question is, "That the words proposed to be added, be there added." Ms Raeesah Khan.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Yet, our sexuality education programmes only teach consent explicitly at the University level and sexuality education at lower levels happens just once or twice a year.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Without consent-focused sexuality education from a young age, our children remain vulnerable to sexual violence – a trauma that can hurt a person for a lifetime.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Sexuality education is a lifelong journey that starts at home and in school.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Open, non-judgmental discussions about consent and respect under a standardised and compulsory national curriculum are essential, as are safe spaces and bystander training from an early age.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This will help our children grow up to be responsible, aware adults and make Singapore a safe and nurturing home for all.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The PAP Women's Wing and Young PAP released a Joint Paper last week on Women's Development that includes a review of sexuality education.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I am glad to see this consensus on our need to update sexuality education and look forward to more conversations on such updates.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Persons with intellectual disabilities, too, have often been victims of sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Closer to home, a man was charged in November last year for sexually assaulting his 17-year-old intellectually disabled daughter when her mother was not home.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This March, a woman was jailed for sexually assaulting her daughter's intellectually disabled schoolmate on several occasions.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: These cases surfaced as the first victim's teacher had noticed something was amiss and the second victim had reported the incidents to social workers.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As with all sexual assault cases, it is likely that many more go unreported.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I hope that studies can be done on this issue so we can better protect our Singaporeans with intellectual disabilities from violence and its resulting trauma.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Where possible, we should also seek to improve training for teachers, social workers and others who may interact with these vulnerable individuals, to help them better identify potential cases of abuse and sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As we improve our policies targeted at preventing sexual violence, it is just as important for us to improve support for survivors.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The suicide of a South Korean female air force officer, three months after she had been sexually assaulted and pressured to cover it up, is a powerful reminder of the cost of turning a blind eye to survivors and their needs.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In the case of Nicholas Lim, who filmed a fellow female student while she was showering, the survivor shared with the public that she did not receive much support.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: While many institutions have since moved to improve their support structures for survivors of sexual violence, this has likely varied among institutions.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It is incredible to see the emergence of more ground-up initiatives, including safe spaces and support groups for victims of sexual assault.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In my line of work, I have accompanied people to Police stations to make reports on sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It is already incredibly difficult for survivors to feel comfortable making a report in the first place, but sometimes the responses from those called to protect us can be disheartening.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Three years ago, I accompanied a 25-year-old survivor to make a Police report against a rape that was committed against her.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The Police officer had allegedly made comments about her dressing and the fact that she was drinking.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need better treatment of survivors of sexual assault and sexual harassment by law enforcement.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In recent years, we have seen training rolled out for judges and regulations for how lawyers argue sexual assault cases – all steps in the right direction to prevent re-victimisation.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Survivor-centered care is a crucial step in addressing sexual violence and our Police officers can also be supported by counsellors or trained mental health personnel at Police stations other than the Onesafe Centre in Police Cantonment Complex.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Assuring survivors that they can be taken seriously and not blamed for the horrors that they have faced is an important step of making our law enforcement system more just.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This will help build confidence in the sensitivity and capacity of law enforcement to handle difficult issues delicately, and will encourage more victims of sexual violence to come forward.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: While I acknowledge that providing more victim support and increased reporting will require more resources on the part of law enforcement, I believe that this is something we must commit to.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: No victim should ever feel like those with the power to safeguard them have disregarded their needs.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It has not escaped the notice of the foreign press, such as Reuters and the BBC, or even local activists working on this issue.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Many of my friends in the Malay/Muslim community have gone through this practice themselves.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: While there are many facets to this complex issue, I wish today to solely focus on the medical and health implications of the practice.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As recently as 20 years ago, FGC was performed by traditional midwives in homes with no sterilisation or anaesthesia.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Today, I understand that the procedure is mostly performed by doctors in private clinics.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The cut ranges from a symbolic placement of scissors or a penknife on the intended organ, or a nick, but the most common form of cutting in Singapore still involves some removal of genital tissue.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Anecdotal experiences reveal an over-cutting or laceration of other parts of the vulva.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Considering that the typical size of a baby girl’s vulva is a mere 1.5 centimetre, this may lead to a disproportionate loss of nerve endings and the creation of scar tissue.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, as with any invasive medical procedure, there is always a chance of infection.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Female genital cutting may also hurt a baby’s attachment to her caregiver.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: A study by the Washington University School of Medicine found that a common defence mechanism of the nervous system to pain is to shut down, which negatively affects interactions with the caregiver.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: A second potential negative mental health impact is on childhood brain development.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Exposure to acute pain in babies and children activates biological stress responses, which may hinder optimal development.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Even if they process it differently from adults, babies still face the risk of long-term physical and mental health implications – as well as strained bonds with their parents – with female genital cutting.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In a reply to the BBC article, a representative of MUIS said it "does not condone any procedures which bring harm to the individual", adding that the Council has "always held the position that female genital cutting should be avoided".

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The counselling process will allow for doctors to first assess if a baby is medically fit to undergo the procedure, as well as to educate parents on the potential risks.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The counselling can also serve to make sure neither parent is being coerced to comply with the practice, either by their spouse, relatives or external parties.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The decision to proceed should be unanimous and there should be measures in place to ensure that the procedure is being done with the knowledge of both parents.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This will help us understand the potential medical risks faced by those who undergo the procedure.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, only in marriages under the Registry of Muslim Marriages (RMM) are men allowed to marry more than one wife, and even up to four wives at one time.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Our regulations stipulate that each application is rigorously reviewed by the RMM, and that it is only approved if "there’s an urgent reason or necessity" or a "good reason" for the subsequent marriages.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Recently, a community initiative called Lepak Conversations did a survey on multiple issues pertaining to gender equality.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Their survey found that even though regulations here may be stricter than in other countries, many men still marry their subsequent wives abroad, ignoring the need for an approval letter from the state.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In 2014, it was reported that more than 100 Singaporean men underwent a second, unregistered marriage in Indonesia.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Growing up, I remember having a conversation with one of my classmates in Primary school about how her father had decided to marry another wife in Batam against her mother’s wishes.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This caused a huge financial strain on her family and her home environment grew increasingly unstable.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: She would come to school crying and found it difficult to concentrate on her studies.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Polygamy does not only affect the man in the relationship, it also affects women and children.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In Islam, the desired outcomes to teachings are generally for us to bring good to society.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: However, we see that some effects of polygamy are clearly negative.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: While the Government cannot do much about individuals who leave Singapore to marry additional wives, the fact that polygamy is allowed under the law reinforces its cultural acceptance, serving as a justification for those who skirt the regulations.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In countries like Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Tunisia and Turkey, polygamy is banned.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Measures must be taken to ensure that this consent is given willingly rather than under coercion.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, we can adopt a rebuttable legal presumption that an applicant cannot be fair and/or provide equally for both his existing and potential wives.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This leaves the law in place, but ends polygamy in practice.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In these ways, the Government can discourage the practice more intentionally before prohibiting it completely.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: On top of this, measures should be put in place that discourage men from attempting to skirt the law by registering marriages abroad.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: There are many contributors to gender equality and one of them is financial liberation.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: How do we ensure that gender does not hamper each of us from being able to support ourselves?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The lack of inclusive workplaces, especially for women who wear the hijab, remains a powerful barrier to women today.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The hijab, to many women, is sacred and represents a deeply personal relationship that they have with their religion.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Though there are many schools of thought in Islam on the necessity of various degrees of modesty, for some, covering the head is an essential part of their Muslim identity and practice.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this year, in this House, my colleague Mr Faisal Manap brought up the very important point that COVID-19 has made it a tough time for many.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: People have lost their jobs or have difficulty finding employment, especially women who wear the hijab.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Ms He Ting Ru rightly points out that women are disproportionately affected by this pandemic.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: There are many workplaces that still discriminate against the hijab, such as other uniformed groups.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Recently, New Zealand’s police force introduced the hijab as part of its uniform.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The government of the day sets the tone on acceptance and tolerance at times.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: If our uniformed services do not pledge to create inclusive spaces, it shows Singaporeans, especially those in the private sector, that they too can discriminate.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I understand that for some Singaporeans, the hijab may be a divisive topic.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: To combat this, we need to educate our society on the various forms of religious expression.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Instead of hiding or pushing them aside, we must encourage Singaporeans to embrace our differences.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We must interrogate our preconceived notions and stereotypes against minority races, so that we do not judge each other superficially.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Only this will truly lead to the unity in diversity that we strive for as a multicultural nation.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I wish to conclude with a story that touched me while I was on one of my house visits.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I met a young five-year-old girl being cared for by her grandmother whilst her parents got a much-needed break.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The grandmother invited me in and made me some delicious bandung, while the girl chatted away to me, sharing with me her many interests, including her obsession with planes!

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: She told me that one day she would like to be a pilot and fly planes high in the sky.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: When I think about gender equality, I think about her and the barriers being broken down even now.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Not so long ago, female pilots were non-existent and even now they are rare.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: But how wonderful is it to think that we have the opportunity to continue breaking down these barriers, so girls like her too can have limitless dreams.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This is what I feel is the crux of this Motion.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I call all of us in this House to work towards fulfilling the aspirations of Singapore women.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Out of five children, only one is a boy.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Needless to say, I grew up in an environment of outspoken females who never feared making their opinions known.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, I wonder how my brother feels being sandwiched between all these female voices.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: My mother was the pillar of our family, a homemaker running a tight ship at home.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She made sure we ate, did well in school, but also that we had fun.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, she also instilled in us that the Malay/Muslim woman was a capable woman.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She is someone who is independent, courageous and who is of value to the world.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In Islamic history, we have countless examples of inspiring women such as Khadijah, who was both a successful businesswoman and mother.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Or Amra bin Al-Rahman, a well-known jurist who tutored many famous scholars and was described as a boundless ocean of knowledge.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Closer to home, according to Population Census 2020, females, in general, have advanced more rapidly in educational attainment.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, more Malay females are attending University as compared to Malay males.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is more that can be done to encourage and enable the success of young Malay/Muslim women.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is a cause that I feel strongly about.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In many Asian countries, women are traditionally seen to be the caregivers of society while the men take the role of the breadwinners.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, this delineation of roles has blurred with the rise of dual-income couples.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This increase is also reflected in the Malay community.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, an equal share of household responsibilities is ideal.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What usually happens, though, is a role overload in which an employed woman is expected to fulfil the traditional role as a homemaker, as well as juggle her career.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In dire situations, when push comes to shove in a family, the female is also expected to sacrifice their career to assume the role of caregiver in society.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted our economic and social activities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With more of the workforce working from home, traditional gender stereotypes have resulted in women taking on added responsibilities at home, such as taking charge of their children's home-based learning.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With these dire statistics, how do we ensure that our Malay/Muslim female youths are able to get the support they need to overcome these difficulties?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Women should be encouraged to mentor the younger generation and support them in their endeavours.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The mentoring scheme can be organised through the community self-help groups where several initiatives are already in place to create safe spaces for women, or even informal networks.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Muslim Women's Association is also embarking on its journey to create a one-stop resource space to enable women to increase their knowledge and skills in various domains: legal, religious, workforce skills and so on.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, through my work with the Young Women in Leadership Dialogue (YWILD), I have met many inspiring Malay/Muslim female youths.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Being a woman, much less from a minority community, may bring about its own set of challenges, but these women have shown courage and grace in the face of adversity.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They also embody success in many forms, whether in academics, sports or activism.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Take Aida Saad, an artist whose art exhibitions and installations raise awareness of individuals with Down's Syndrome and allows the public to see the world through their lenses.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She is feted as a rising artist by the National Arts Council.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Or Nur Aziemah Azman, a former madrasah student and a graduate of the prestigious Al-Azhar University.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: She is currently an Associate Research Fellow at the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS).

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Today, her mastery in multiple languages, as well as her research expertise in the domains of online extremism, international terrorism, religion and identity has given her team an edge in safeguarding Singapore's security.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: YWILD also aims to provide a platform for young women in our community to have those difficult conversations regarding gender and apply it within the context and value system of the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, we need a whole-of-society and community mindset shift to re-educate the society on shared responsibilities in the home.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we need to involve the young and old, our boys and their caregivers in this conversation too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Just this year, The Straits Times produced a video called InstaSex that delved into the stories of teens who encountered sexual harassment and physical assault as a result of interactions on social media.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, there was an online poll sexualising ustazah, or female Islamic religious teachers, with a view to committing sexual violence against them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Internet has added a layer of anonymity that may embolden some to use it as a platform to denigrate women.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These incidents should not be chalked up to people being oversensitive.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This underscores the relevance and significance of the work of the Alliance for Action Committee formed to tackle online harms.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Teach them to not make light of casual remarks that belittle women so that it does not become normalised, and teach them to stand up to those who do.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Treat the boys with compassion so that they may become compassionate boys too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we need to involve the young and old, our boys and their caregivers in this conversation too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Teach them to not make light of casual remarks that belittle women, so it does not become normalised and teach them to stand up to those who do.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Treat the boys with compassion so they may become compassionate boys too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And women, we are allies of each other too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): And women, we are allies of each other too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I am confident that the results of such efforts will be far-reaching and worthwhile, and I look forward to it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, let me thank the Singapore Muslim Women's Association for their contributions to this speech.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, even then, there are certain ridges and differences within these very movements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some invoke race; others invoke class; and sometimes, these movements discount, if not cannibalise one another.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, a house divided against itself cannot stand, and this cannot be for the case of elevating and empowering women, especially in a year we have declared the Year of Celebrating SG Women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I know even as I stand here speaking in Parliament today about a Motion on women's interests, submitted also by a woman, that we are all standing on the shoulders of giants.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Broad are the shoulders of the sisters who have gone before us and there is always space for more.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We welcome the solidarity the Workers' Party has shown, picking up arms to join our ongoing ascent to elevating and empowering women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Willing to listen, willing to put in the hard work and willing to look ahead.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are principles on which the Labour Movement has moved to organise our society's resources and shake up cultural mindsets to elevate and empower our Singaporean women in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this movement for women workers we have forged, I would like to remind us of its decades-long importance as we look to chart the next few decades to come for our women in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On being willing to listen: the year is 1973, and women are stepping up in full force to work in paid employment roles, especially with exciting foreign direct investments flowing into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Much like today, women were going on the ascent in their own right, and the taste of empowerment gave us the confidence and momentum to traverse through barriers that might have still stood in our way.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She said, "Through the Central Committee, I hope to bring about parity treatment with equal wage for equal work for women".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Annabella and her team of unionists started their journey with an ear to the ground, consulting with working women to identify their primary concerns.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They discovered that after making their first forays into the workforce, women would often leave their jobs after starting a family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This was merely what was expected of us in the household then as women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our unionists and sisters listened, and they took to heart.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This birthed out pioneering efforts by women in the Labour Movement to provide childcare support and helping women rejoin the workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement started NTUC Childcare in 1977 to shoulder the burdens of women who felt the need to leave their jobs early on in their careers without support for childcare.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC Childcare scaled the number of these childcare centres to double-digit figures within a couple years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We drove fundraising efforts to establish new centres, as well as contended for Government subsidies to keep childcare fees easily affordable for parents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Pioneering and building our childcare infrastructure was no small feat and this is an ongoing work-in-progress.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2019, our Women's Wing put up a position paper titled "Supporting Parenthood and Young Families".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Prime Minister acknowledged the importance of a good preschool and how it provides many long-term benefits in life, and the Government has steadily improved the accessibility, affordability and quality of preschools.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The long-term plan is to cap our preschool fees so that the full-day childcare will be the same as Primary school fees plus after student care fees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On being willing to look ahead: in the mid-2000s, Singapore was met with a sustained shortage of labour, as well as an ageing population problem looming around the corner.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not only was this a golden opportunity for us to usher women back into the workforce, but it needed to be delicately balanced with strong support for women to start families.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement has helped women re-enter the workplace as early as the 1990s, and through the years, we have evolved our programmes to keep with the zeitgeist of the times.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Director of the Women’s Programme back then, our President Halimah Yacob and the Women’s Committee started a Back-to-Work (B2W) Programme in 2007 to create new opportunities for women in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The programme, with a robust strategy, including recruitment, re-adjustment and retention plans for women’s return to the workforce, was intended for the benefit of future generations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With its introduction, we saw the consolidation of best practices in training, counselling and job placements, as well as the promotion of flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With these best practices, we fuelled the Employment and Employability Institute to do its good work in matching workers and employers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With this forward-looking vision, we promoted companies to provide facilities for breastfeeding mothers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, building and evolving on the work the Labour Movement has advocated for, flexible work arrangements are the new norm, and we continue to work with our tripartite partners to implement and redesign jobs to enable women to return to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For progressive companies with the Labour Movement family, they are guided by workplace harassment clauses in their collective agreements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our unions and women leaders represent both women and men in harassment and grievance cases.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We continue to listen, work hard and prepare for the new work norms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are only eating the fruits of the trees planted by those who have come before us and we will continue to plant trees for those to come.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The enterprise, tenacity and vision of our women who had gone before us, indeed, lay the foundation for the work we continue today and we are glad to have reinforcements even across party lines to continue their good work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we consider the Motion filed for a whole-of-society approach in empowering women, we say "Let us do it".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And let us continue to do it the way we have been doing it for years – being willing to listen, willing to put in the hard work and willing to look ahead.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These core principles will continue to shape our success.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Decades later, though the challenges women face have evolved in form due to the myriad opportunities made available to women, we must continue to put our ears to the ground, be good listeners and be able to roll with the punches.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Policy measures that look good on paper sometimes only look good because they are overly convenient and fail to consider repercussions downstream.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To this, we say let us continue to innovate solutions and undertake them even if they seem difficult, because that is the diligence our women deserve.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While whole societies begin to elevate and empower women, women begin to elevate whole societies to greater heights than before.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was an increase of almost 2,000 applications from the year before.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These extensions are typically for one to three months, but some are reportedly as short as one or two weeks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A number of my constituents have sought assistance regarding renewals of STVPs and applications for Long-Term Visit Passes (LTVPs) for their foreign spouses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am sure many Members would have also submitted such appeals to ICA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the majority of cases that I have come across, the foreign spouse is a woman.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They face the uncertainty and anxiety of being separated from their Singaporean husbands and, in some cases, their children as well, if their passes are not renewed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have also noticed that almost all of the residents who have approached me for assistance with their spouses’ visas are from lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Applications for STVP extensions cost $40 for every three months of stay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While it might not seem much, this adds up over time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, their spouses’ immigration worries often add to their daily stresses of life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To reduce the immigration-related stressors faced by Singapore Citizens and their foreign spouses, I propose the creation of a more streamlined path towards obtaining LTVP, LTVP+ and PR status and, eventually, citizenship for such spouses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are strong reasons for such a policy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, given that a quarter of marriages here are between a Singaporean and a non-resident, transnational marriages will continue to be an important contributor to family formation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As such, fast-tracking parents and potential parents of Singaporean children for citizenship would facilitate the formation of stable family units with a full stake in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Towards this end, the primary consideration for PR applications by LTVP holders who have a Singaporean spouse or child, should be their family ties and rootedness in Singapore and not just their income or occupation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their close family relationship with Singaporeans makes them part of the Singapore Core and we should facilitate, not inhibit, their integration into our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that not all foreign spouses may immediately qualify for PR status.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, foreigners who have entered into a bona fide marriage with a Singapore citizen should be granted LTVP status by default.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have constituents who have been married to foreigners for over a year and are still unable to obtain an LTVP for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They need to continually renew their spouse’s STVPs, with no certainty of approval each time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One constituent told me of his desire to have children with his wife but he has shelved those plans because he is worried that his wife may be forced to leave Singapore if her pass is not extended, leading to a separation from any children they might have.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to appeal for the Government to raise the level of support currently given to single parents, so that they and their children are not disadvantaged in our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In a speech in 2013, I outlined the burdens faced by single parents who have to take on the role of both father and mother and perform caregiving duties while also holding on to a job to pay the bills.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Compounding their challenges, they are denied some of the parenthood benefits that married, divorced and widowed parents receive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could add to their feeling of marginalisation from society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since single mothers make up the bulk of single parents, changes to policies to support single parents will disproportionately benefit women.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My former Parliamentary colleagues, in particular, Ms Lee Li Lian, as well as Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, Mr Png Eng Huat, and current Members Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap, Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Leon Perera and others, have repeatedly advocated for greater support for single parents over the past eight years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Government benefits and housing options for single unmarried parents and their children should be the same as for any other family unit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The distinction that the Government often makes between single unmarried parents and divorced parents, in terms of the benefits provided, should be removed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, we should not encourage single parenthood or having children outside of marriage, any more than we encourage divorce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is hard enough raising children with both parents, let alone by oneself.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, once a woman has made the brave choice to carry her child to term despite not having the support of a spouse and likely family disapproval, we, as a society, must do all we can to support her.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should not make things more difficult for her by denying her benefits available to other parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must also be mindful that unequal benefits inadvertently penalise the innocent children of single unmarried parents, who are often in need of greater support.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What this means in practice – and I have seen this among my constituents – is that they and their children have to squeeze into a flat with their parents, close relatives or friends.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If they fall out with their family members or are estranged from their families – as some are – they risk having nowhere to stay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Renting a flat in the open market is seldom a realistic option as it is prohibitively expensive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that HDB has said that it will exercise flexibility in allowing unmarried parents to buy a 3-room or smaller flat in a non-mature estate from HDB, or a resale flat, and that those who cannot afford to buy a flat may be considered for public rental flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All single parents and their children are a family in every sense of the word and should be considered a family nucleus by HDB for the purpose of purchasing or renting flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some single parents who are divorcees also continue to face difficulties getting their monthly maintenance from their former spouses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government introduced the Maintenance Record Office (MRO) scheme in 2016 to assist the Courts in identifying those who refuse to pay even though they have the means to do so, so that the Courts can impose penalties on them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Leon Perera previously asked in 2017 if MSF could provide a mechanism for spouses to request an investigation of the MRO without having to go through the Court process.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry will give consideration to this proposal as it reviews the MRO programme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I should also mention that we should give single fathers the same benefits as single mothers, as they face very similar challenges as single mothers in raising their children alone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Women’s Charter was changed in 2016 to allow men to apply for alimony.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this is only possible if he is incapacitated and, therefore, unable to work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The final point I wish to raise relates to work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I call for companies to redouble their efforts to make flexible work arrangements available to employees who can and wish to work from home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government can do its part to nudge enterprises in this direction through tax incentives and by leading the way through Civil Service human resource policies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I recently met an elderly constituent at the wake of her deceased husband.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As was my usual practice, I asked if she was in need of any assistance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was glad to hear that she was doing fine as she was able to continue working from home because of the arrangements made by her enlightened employer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Her employer couriers her work to her flat daily and picks it up from her the next morning after she has completed it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This way, despite her inability to walk very far unassisted, she can still apply her skills and earn some income to support herself.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe that more businesses should explore such flexible work arrangements to meet their manpower needs while providing employment to those who can only work from home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will empower many women with caregiving responsibilities, not to mention older workers and those with mobility issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are many women as well as some men who make the difficult choice to stop work temporarily to care for their young children or elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Very often, this dilemma could have been avoided if more companies allowed their employees to work from home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One silver lining of the COVID-19 pandemic is that it has forced many companies to digitalise and make work-from-home arrangements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This has been helpful for many caregivers who need to look after their young children or elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, once Singapore starts to reopen, many companies may start summoning their workers back to the office.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope companies will not forgo their digital gains this way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Companies should assess which jobs can be performed as productively at home as in the office and give employees a choice of working remotely.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The gap starts to form for women starting from their mid-20s– the age when they start having children – and continues to increase throughout their childbearing years, with a peak of some 25% behind men of the same age.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could point to what is known as the "child penalty", which could have a negative impact on a woman’s earning power and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even with work-from-home arrangements, SMU sociologist Aliya Rao found that women bear a greater burden of handling both paid work as well as unpaid work of managing the household.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a point that Ms He Ting Ru also made earlier.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to promote a work environment that is more understanding of the various roles that mothers and fathers desire to play and avoid forcing them to choose one role over the other.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will enable many more parents to continue pursuing their careers while providing for themselves and caring for their families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In summary, Madam, I call for the streamlining of immigration procedures for foreign spouses of Singapore Citizens to strengthen the Singapore Core; for more support to be extended to single unmarried parents; and for policies to promote flexible work arrangements, all of which will benefit both women and men.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For such questions, we would like to request that she gives us specific details, even through a Parliamentary Question, so that this can be looked into and we can give her a proper answer for these questions.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan
text: Like I mentioned, it was three years ago and I do not wish to re-traumatise the person that I had accompanied.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan
text: But I have to say that these anecdotes are not isolated.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan
text: Perhaps, this can start further discussions on how victims or survivors are treated after they make reports.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I know that it is not going to be easy for you or even for the victim to go through this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: But from the Police's point of view, you have just made a very important allegation and we would like to have the details to look into it further.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I was listening intently to the speeches of hon Member Ms He Ting Ru and several of the Workers' Party Members earlier and found their points made to be quite similar to the suggestions made by my fellow PAP Members of Parliament over the years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, Ms He Ting Ru today asked for greater representation of females at the leadership level for greater diversity of views.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, in 2017, several Members of this House, including Mdm Deputy Speaker yourself, hon Members Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Alex Yam, Mr Louis Ng and several others have called for the same.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ms He Ting Ru also raised the point on CPF transfers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This was also a point that was raised by several of our Members, including Ms Joan Pereira, former Member of Parliament Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar, in 2017 and there were several efforts before that as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There was also a suggestion or a call for the gender-neutral CareShield Life premium.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I think this one – several Members, including myself – also called for this in 2018 and, again, in 2019.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, indeed, I am very heartened to observe this because this reinforces the recommendations that we had put forth as well, as we all desire to support Singapore women in realising their fullest potential.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am also heartened that, so far, nobody has objected to the amendments as moved by hon Member Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I, therefore, take it that it is a recognition that we need to go beyond this debate and have it translated into something that is actionable for the future, as set out in the upcoming White Paper.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, this House has, over the past six to seven decades, seen many exchanges and recommendations on how we can empower and advance Singapore women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling earlier recounted the key milestones in this long journey towards removing barriers and empowering Singapore women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I was heartened that 18 Members of the House, including me, spoke on this important cause and that our Ministers and Ministers of State gave so much of their time to address our concerns and recommendations, and echoed their support for the aspirations of Singapore women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I certainly appreciated the interest and support from the Workers' Party in the 2017 Motion debate as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Colleagues who called for this included Ms Joan Pereira, Miss Cheryl Chan and Minister of State Sun Xueling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, we called for platforms and cogent programmes to refresh and build new capabilities to help back-to-work women because these expand their capacities to pursue the diverse aspirations that they may have.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ms Jessica Tan, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Darryl David, Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar and Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam spoke very passionately on this in 2017.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The second strategy was to provide options for women so that ladies with career aspirations do not have to feel that they need to sacrifice or feel guilty about having to juggle different roles and feel inadequate at any point in time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A wide range of recommendations, including flexible work arrangements, were raised by almost all the Members of Parliament who spoke.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, Miss Cheryl Chan and Mr Darryl David called for progressive human resource policies and practices to complement the many recommendations put forth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Members of Parliament, such as Ms Joan Pereira, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam, Mr Alex Yam and Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar, called for CPF top-ups for women who gave up their careers to stay at home to care for their family members.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The third strategy was to remove barriers, especially the ones that were often stereotypical and pigeonhole women in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Members, including Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Louis Ng spoke passionately about how women were under-represented at the board and executive levels and how we should also drive up women's participation and leadership within the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to do so, we need to recognise the stereotypes and biases constraining women in those different roles.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mr Darryl David, Mr Louis Ng, Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar and, certainly, Mr Leon Perera talked about the need to shift the care burden to have a more equal sharing of care duties between men and women, whether it is at the workplace, in the family or even within the social setting.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, Ms Jessica Tan also reminded everyone to be conscious of our unconscious bias so that women will not be inevitably disadvantaged from the start of recruitment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The fourth strategy was to be future-ready – to have smart women for a smart nation – something that I felt and continue to be passionate about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We called for digital fluency, the use of smart solutions to create capacity and empowering women with science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education so that they are well-positioned for the job opportunities in growth sectors and leap towards closing that gender pay gap.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This recommendation is again reiterated in the paper jointly authored by the PAP Women's Wing and Young PAP submitted this year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Taken together, the debate demonstrated from both sides of the House our support for the aspirations of Singapore women and the willingness of this Government to support likewise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Between the debate in 2017 till now, I am encouraged to observe several positive developments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To facilitate inter-generational bonding, the first inter-generational playground and infant and childcare centre within a nursing home was launched in late 2017.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since then, we have witnessed eldercare and childcare facilities being co-located in new HDB estates.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MacPherson Spring in my constituency is an example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe such co-location of facilities offers much convenience to caregivers taking care of the young and old in their families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, in addition to increasing the availability of these care places, subsidies also play a very important role to help making it a lot more accessible to working fathers and mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this respect, I am glad to note that childcare, infant care subsidies have been enhanced in 2020, that is, last year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On flexible work arrangements, we know from a January 2021 written Parliamentary response to Mr Christopher de Souza that the vast majority of employees today, including caregivers, have access to flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That is why many colleagues, like Dr Tan Wu Meng, for example, today continue to champion this, as evident by his Parliamentary Questions in this House just earlier today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In empowering more girls with STEM education, I am encouraged that female representation in Information Technology courses in local Universities has increased from 28% in 2017 to 35% in 2019.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And pushing further to avail Singapore women of good career opportunities, the PAP called for greater help for women to secure jobs in growth sectors as we recognise that there are tech-lite jobs suitable for those without a STEM background within the tech sector, and demand for workers remains strong in the care and green economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, I am glad to participate in the debate on this meaningful Motion today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The contributions of Singapore women to the family, community and country are evident to all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since I entered Parliament in 2011, I have heard many suggestions from my colleagues on issues related to support for women in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have also witnessed the implementation of Government policies to help women in Singapore achieve greater progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In 2017, I had the honour to move a Motion with four of my fellow Members of Parliament in Parliament on how to help Singaporean women realise their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With 13 other Members of Parliament, we engaged in a two-day debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The debate in 2017 outlined four key strategies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, create and strengthen frameworks and services to share the burden of caregivers and free up time for them to better balance their multiple roles.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, to promote flexible work arrangements and give them options to care for their families without sacrificing their careers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, encourage society and businesses to value women's economic potential and contributions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, promote skills training for women in science and technology to prepare them for the digital age and the future economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, the suggestions put forward were not confined to women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My colleagues and I had hoped to seek your support through the Motion to support our women with concrete actions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will no doubt strengthen Singapore's foundations and help Singaporeans, both men and women, to develop their potential and prepare for the future together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since 2017, we have made progress in many areas, including eldercare, childcare, flexible work arrangements and digital education and training.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, the number of home care places has increased 30% between 2017 and 2019, while day care and childcare places rose by 80% and 11% respectively in the same period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For more than 60 years, we have been fighting for more support for women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today's Motion is built on this solid foundation and is an added effort.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With each wave of industrial revolution, renewal of skills in the workplace, changes in the general environment and societal attitudes, we have to keep up with the changes and make corresponding adjustments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe this is why the Government announced last year that it would jointly organise Conversations on Singapore Women’s Development with partners in the private and public sectors, and consolidate the recommendations into a White Paper which will be submitted to Parliament this year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: AWARE and the Workers' Party have also submitted their proposals.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, the contributions of Singapore women to the family and society cannot be overlooked.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must press on to support women in realising their potential and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I look forward to the release of the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): This journey to support Singapore women fulfil their fullest potential and aspirations is not new.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even as I speak of the 2017 debate, there were many others before me in this House who had championed the cause.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And I am glad that we are building on this firm foundation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are many things we can still do to support Singapore women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the broader environment changes, as demographics and societal attitudes shift, we need to adjust, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Question: how does Singapore fare right now in women political leadership?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe we all accept that women must be a big part of this House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Women must not just be a big part of this House; women should hold leadership positions in Government and in political parties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, this House has seen progress.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For decades before 1984, the House was all male.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After the 1984 General Elections, three women were elected on the ruling party ticket – Dr Aline Wong, Dr Dixie Tan and Mrs Yu-Foo Yee Shoon.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They made up about 3% of the total number of Members of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, the House is touching 30% women, a 10-fold increase.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have female Ministers, we had a female Speaker, we continue to have female Leaders of the House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How are we doing if we compare ourselves globally?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) puts out a country ranking of the percentage of females in national legislatures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When one looks at the countries above Singapore, they are an incredibly diverse mix of countries at different stages of development.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are doing slightly better than the USA at 27% and about on par with Germany and Australia which are at 31%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When one looks at the list of countries with high proportions of women legislators, one will notice that certain countries which are not known for gender equality seem to be high on the list.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, while the numbers matter, we should not have women fill places in Parliaments for its own sake, if they do not play a meaningful role.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order to reach 30%, some family-run companies may be tempted to appoint female family members, but that would not be meaningful if these women did not exercise independent decision-making.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, it is somewhat reassuring to see that in Singapore politics, there is an increased presence of women playing influential roles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are more female Ministers in Cabinet than ever before, helming Ministries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also more female opposition Members of Parliament than ever before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We want to see more of them, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But what will it take to increase the pool of able and willing female Singaporeans entering the forefront of politics?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Any political leader in Singapore will know that it is more difficult to find women to stand as candidates in Parliamentary elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I count myself fortunate that I did not face any family or societal pressures when I decided to join the Workers’ Party 20 years ago.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not having a spouse or children, I did not need to agonise over how the family would cope without me at home at night, or how their lives and morale would be affected by nasty media headlines and the testy exchanges that take place in this House from time to time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for my parents, they are persons of great fortitude.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My mother is a retired nurse who has seen life-and-death emergencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for my late father, he simply laughed it off on learning that I had joined the Workers’ Party, saying, and I quote: "Congratulations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Time and again, we find potential female candidates who are unable to freely decide whether to stand as candidates, compared to males who seem to have fewer inhibitions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Workers’ Party is not unique in this experience.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Women, especially those with young children, are burdened with worry and even guilt, wanting to be there for their families at key moments of their children’s development.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The expectations of family members, particularly parents and parents-in-law, add more pressure to mothers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Employers, too, may doubt a working mother’s ability to cope with her work and political responsibilities as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not notice such pressure and apprehension in my dealings with potential male candidates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I should clarify, at this point, that I am not saying that a woman who decides that her family is the most important thing to her is somehow under-achieving or under-contributing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What I am saying is that we should empower women to freely make these choices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Women should be confident that, in their ecosystem, family responsibilities are shared.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They should be confident that their contributions to the wider society are cheered and supported, and not seen as derelictions of their duties as mothers, daughters and daughters-in-law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some countries have tried to boost female participation in their legislatures through the imposition of legal quotas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am personally very wary of going down this route, which has led to some perverse outcomes elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I learned of this a few years ago when I was part of a Commonwealth delegation observing a national election on the African continent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Several female politicians shared that their experience with legal quotas had not been good.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Their national elections had proportional representation systems of affirmative action for women.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Political parties would put up lists of female candidates, who would be assured of entering Parliament depending on their party’s overall vote share at the polls.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, more countries seem to have had sustainable success with soft targets or aspirational quotas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These voluntary targets serve as benchmarks to aim towards, without being overly rigid in application.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some countries saw political parties voluntarily setting party quotas, promising the electorate that they would field at least a certain percentage of women candidates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This happened due to political competition, as political parties jostled to gain support from a more demanding electorate and, especially, from female voters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although political parties in Singapore have not announced any voluntary quotas of women candidates, my observation is that the parties are, indeed, conscious of the need to field at least a minimum proportion of women.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the Progress Singapore Party, they fielded about 21% of female candidates and, after Polling Day, two Non-Constituency Members of Parliament were elected – one man and one woman.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the decision-making levels of the parties, the Central Executive Committees (CECs) of both the PAP and the WP are still male-dominated, but to different degrees at the moment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PAP has three female CEC members out of 18, making up about 17%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The WP CEC has four women out of 14, making up 29%; though this is a vast improvement from the 14% we had previously, I am most mindful that this gain is precarious and can easily unravel.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PSP has five women out of a 14-member CEC, a healthy 36%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems to me that all political parties can put in more effort to try to raise the levels of female participation in leadership.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am cautiously optimistic that we may not need to adopt even voluntary quotas to improve the situation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As has happened in other countries, the element of competition amongst political parties in Singapore will also result in the need for parties to field more women candidates and promote women leadership.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
