text: However, given the social context, it will not be an easy slog unless the whole of society embraces policies which make it conducive for women to step up to the political forefront.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now turn to the relevance of gender equality in society to fostering increased female participation in politics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is thus relevant to ask whether a society that nurtures a gender-neutral culture will organically see more women in politics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Gender equality assessments across countries are regularly done, and there are reports and rankings of gender gaps worldwide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in March this year, the World Bank published the Global Gender Gap Report 2021.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This report assesses gender gaps in countries across four fields – political empowerment, economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, and health and survival.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of all the four fields assessed, political empowerment is the one with the largest gender gap worldwide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If one looks at the top 10 countries deemed to be the most gender neutral, one sees that eight out of these 10 are also in the top 25 for female representation in their parliaments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These include the usual suspects such as the Nordic countries, as well as New Zealand, Namibia and Rwanda.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: An academic study of 36 European countries was published last year which attempted to test certain hypotheses as to why countries might have higher or lower percentages of women in their parliaments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The study tested two hypotheses – the first was whether higher percentages of women parliamentarians were found in richer countries measured by GDP per capita; the second was whether the proportion of women parliamentarians was co-related with the country's character as measured on a Masculinity Index.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Masculinity Index was determined based on a variety of factors such as: the importance of money, high economic growth as a priority, men earning more than women and traditional family structures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such masculine traits were to be contrasted with the Femininity Index which valued caring for others and the quality of life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore was ranked in the middle of this scale.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The study found that a higher proportion of women in parliament was strongly co-related with a country's wealth but also with a low score on the Masculinity Index.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Three Nordic countries – Norway, Finland and Sweden – exemplify this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, more equal sharing of childcare and eldercare responsibilities will ease decision-making for women.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Wage levels should be comparable for equivalent work, so that it may make economic sense for husbands to decide to work part-time or not at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore should continue in this direction if we wish to see sustained streams of women contributing to their full potential, including those who will step forward to serve as political candidates, Members of Parliament and Ministers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order to attract more women into political leadership, we need all segments of society to work together to build a gender-equal ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That is the spirit in which the whole of society can collaborate in the national interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allow me, if I may, to contribute to this discussion from the economic point of view.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unsurprisingly, discrimination of any form, whether on the basis of race, religion or gender, entails not just visible costs to the social and moral fabric of society, it also embeds hidden or, at least, under-appreciated, costs for the functioning of our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this speech, I wish to bring some of these potentially hidden costs to light.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is now a substantial body of evidence pointing to the importance of gender equality for economic development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Economic historians have argued that one of the important contributors to the Great Divergence, when European Civilization was able to overtake Qing China, Mughal India and Tokugawa Japan, and the difference was the so-called "European Marriage Pattern": a pattern of delayed female marriage, elevated female celibacy and the formation of small, nuclear-family households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The idea is that by improving the position of women, this pattern increases both labour force participation and encourages greater investment in human capital, which serves to promote long-term economic growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This argument has since been rigorously tested against data from around the world and the results are clear: greater gender equality tends to be associated with higher growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Remarkably, the relationship works both ways: not only does empowering women benefit development, but development, in and of itself, can also be a force for suppressing gender inequality, which holds the potential for a virtuous circle of ever-greater empowerment, followed by development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Remarkably, this insight that gender equality and female empowerment are a force for economic progress was most pithily expressed not by a paragon of capitalism, but by an icon of communism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In encouraging women to pursue education and work outside of home, Chairman Mao Zedong famously proclaimed that, 妇女能顶半边天 or, literally, "women hold up half the sky", an allusion to how women can, and do, contribute mightily to the success of the economic endeavours of a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Closer to home, Singapore has, like many Newly Industrialised Economies (NIEs) in East Asia, steadily improved the extent to which women are engaged as productive members of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This represents an increase of a little less than a third, which is notable, nevertheless, for an advanced economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also significantly higher than rates among our NIE peers, which average closer to 53%, and also surpasses that of developed southern European nations such as Greece and Italy, where participation hovers in the low to mid-forties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, we have, even in more recent times, managed to encourage the entry of women into formal employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alas, this impressive quantitative success masks some deeper, and possibly more worrisome, pathology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, participation has trended slightly down over the past five years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I am not, by any stretch of the imagination, suggesting that women should always seek to increase their engagement in the workforce, come what may.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, some retreat from working life may well be a calculated choice, reflecting a desire to spend more time in homemaking or the pursuit of other interests, such as hobbies or philanthropy, which may be enabled by higher incomes from the main breadwinner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we should not be blind to the possibility that some of the fastest growing sectors, such as technology, finance and data science, are famously male-dominated, and reduced participation could be symptomatic of the difficulty that women face in breaking into such lucrative professions, thereby inhibiting the further expansion of labour market entry by women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, there remains a significant imbalance in the participation rates of men versus women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, the ratio of female-to-male labour force participation is around 0.79, substantially below Scandinavian countries, where the ratio is closer to 0.9.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, we know that greater egalitarianism is eminently possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another reason that constrains further participation by Singaporean women is that they are still often expected to take on the primary responsibilities of caregiving and housework in the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, asking women to hold down a job and advance in their careers, while also taking on domestic work, effectively consigns women to a double shift, or equivalently, juggling two jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Often, the added burden compels them to either leave the workforce or reduce their hours to part-time employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, women are over-represented in part-time jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This latter statistic underscores the main obstacle preventing greater female labour force participation – time constraints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, working part-time could well be a lifestyle choice I alluded to earlier, which should be available regardless of gender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But with only 47% of firms in Singapore offering full-time, flexible work arrangements, many women find themselves taking on part-time jobs not necessarily by choice, but rather because their employer either refuses or fails to offer alternatives that would allow them to continue working full-time, especially after the birth of the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my meetings with residents, I have had many women express difficulty in convincing their employer to agree to more flexible work arrangements, which relegates them effectively to part-time status.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A third force may discourage women from entering the labour force with more vigour: the gender pay gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, women's career choices and progression paths, based on differences in personality and preferences, along with the values placed on workplace flexibility and societal norms surrounding certain gender roles do affect this difference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To compare durians to durians, it is necessary to account for these observable and explainable differences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is smaller, but still non-trivial; after all, this is the average annual increment over two to three years, which never goes away.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, we do ourselves a disservice if we simply accept that wage differences can be accounted for and, hence, excusable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, as I explained above, a desire for flexibility should be regarded as an accommodation to a woman for taking on the additional, unpaid duties at home, not a perk that would engender – no pun intended – a discount to this worker's salary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, societal norms about the appropriateness of certain jobs for women – such as in tech and finance, as mentioned earlier – can and should be changed, as there is little clear inherent advantage held by those possessing the Y chromosome in performing these jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, these subtle forms of gender discrimination in the workplace – expressed in dollars and cents – remain real and present in the contemporary Singaporean economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 has now presented itself as a genuine opportunity for us to seize upon and rectify this discrimination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On one hand, the pandemic has hit women harder than men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The need to take on an even greater burden of managing the household as they work from home, has meant lower productivity, higher stress and greater burnout.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such feelings of stress experienced by those working from home even outstripped the amounts reported among frontline workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If doing double shift as a woman was already stressful pre-pandemic, how much more difficult would this have been when parents also had to take on additional educational and childcare responsibilities during lockdown periods, such as the circuit breaker in 2020, or Phase Two (Heightened Alert) this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, many women went from a dreaded double shift, to an unbearable triple.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the pandemic has also starkly revealed how working from home was not just plausible, but more than possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It strikes me that firms expecting a return to business-as-usual look increasingly misguided.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Much like how the Black Death permanently catalysed a dramatic realignment of wages in medieval Europe, COVID-19 will induce a comparable rethinking of employer-employee relationships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The future of work may well be irreversibly flexible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the Government follow this trend, then, in institutionalising clear, flexible work arrangements, starting with the Civil Service?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In addition to a four-day work week, which my Sengkang teammate Louis Chua has previously raised in this House, we can consider an alternative work schedule: add an hour to each workday, which adds up to a long weekend every fortnight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am certain that many working mothers and fathers, for that matter, would value the opportunity to spend an additional day with their children, enjoy a long weekend, or even to attend to more mundane chores that are easiest to perform on a weekday.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, ultimately, requires our leadership – our top administrators in the public sector, our civil society visionaries and our captains of private industry – to fully buy into this vision of a gender-neutral workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in the meantime, to get there from here, we will require policy changes, policy nudges; there remains an insufficient number of female leaders to ensure that diversity and inclusion expand organically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is why the demonstration effect from Government is so crucial.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are many practical steps to promote greater gender diversity in corporate leadership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so since, in contrast to electoral representation – as Aljunied Member of Parliament and my colleague, Ms Sylvia Lim, mentioned earlier –  where there is palpable pressure from political competition, similar pressures are often significantly weaker in the corporate world, to the extent that the gender composition of board memberships even matter to the decisive shareholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Under Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, Japan has made enormous strides in increasing the participation of women in its traditionally male-dominated offices, by dramatically expanding childcare facilities for working mothers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, we can consider paid re-entry programmes for mothers and informal caregivers, to ease their re-integration into the workforce, post-childbirth or after a period of time as the primary caregiver.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Programmes can be designed to refresh and update skills, tax relief can be offered to employers that operate successful re-entry programmes, to strengthen incentives for adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when these opportunities have been offered, our women have eagerly answered the call.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2020, more women have taken up board seats in Statutory Boards, companies and institutions of public character.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOM should then go on to publish aggregated and average pay gap information for each industry sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government should also render support to firms – especially smaller ones – for both the routine collection of such data, as well as offer strategies for how such gaps may be reduced in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Indian Nobel Prize-winning economist Amartya Sen observed that India has as many as 100 million "missing women" – as a result, he claimed, of gender-selective abortions – which is a travesty not just on a demographic and economic perspective, but a tragedy from a moral, societal and cultural one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But let us also not be blind to the fact that there are missing women in our workplaces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are also hundreds of thousands of missing women that is a shortcoming that we can and must collectively resolve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Members of this House may know, I have a young daughter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Like every parent, I want her to grow up in the best possible world, one where she is able to pursue her dreams – whatever they may be – independent of whether she happens to possess a Y chromosome or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I hope that we can all agree that this is why all of us need to work together to realise genuine gender equality in our Singaporean workplaces.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Raeesah Khan, you wish to make a clarification?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given all that has been said by both sides of this House, it is clear that we are all in agreement that this Motion needs to make reference to the action plans that are required.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think beyond an affirmation, there needs to be an acknowledgement of past contributions; beyond a declaration, there needs to be concrete steps; and beyond a statement of intent, there needs to be a call to action.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am sure that the Members of this House, like me, are looking forward to the action plans in the upcoming White Paper arising out of the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This year being the Year of Celebrating Singapore Women, it is important for us to remember how far we have come in terms of society and as a nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Conversations on women's advancement in Singapore have been championed by the PAP Women's Wing since their inception and even before that in 1956 when the PAP Women's League was formed by Mdm Chan Choy Siong, one of the first women to be elected into Parliament in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, it is not to be championed by women alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my years of advocating to end domestic violence and championing women empowerment, I strongly believe that men are integral to any conversation regarding women development.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am thus glad that we have seen an overwhelming support from men who also share these same views.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the collation of ground feedback leading up to these set of recommendations, it is heartening to see men lending their voices and joining in our collective efforts to effect positive change.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Past and present PAP Members in this House have also stood up and spoken up for causes that are close to the hearts of women in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Alex Yam spoke on the equality of value and treatment of both working mothers and stay-at-home mothers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Louis Ng championed the causes of women including breastfeeding mothers, single mothers and foreign spouses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Melvin Yong encouraged men to shoulder the burden that women carry at home to strengthen marriages in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Dr Lam Pin Min sought for more flexibility for fathers to take their parental leave entitlement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Dr Ahmad Mohd Magad more than 10 years ago championed steps to empower single mothers and encourage employers to consider flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are many others from past and present Parliament in our nation's history who have done so as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are not just a "Few Good Men"; they represent the goodness in men and there are many more out there.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They have not only championed the cause, but they have also taken actionable steps with the Government to help shape policies and laws that benefit the women and daughters of our nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But laws and policies are not the be-all and end-all.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to shape mindsets and shift attitudes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, we have seen various cases involving the objectification of women and misogynistic views being spread online.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Patriarchal and stereotype mindsets alienate and demean the potential of our daughters, wives and women in our lives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   During this pandemic, we see more family conflicts that may lead to an increase in cases of domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Learning and working from home have become the norm today.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Increased interactions at home and limited physical space can trigger more misunderstandings and household discord.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This may be due to couples having different perceptions about caregiving and spousal roles at home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This perception may stem from patriarchal thinking or preconceptions about the role of wives, mothers or daughters in the home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fathers now want to be more involved in the upbringing and the lives of their children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Allowing flexibility in sharing parental leave will help families that have their own needs when facing very distinct challenges.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because not everyone can work from home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With a deeper involvement of fathers, this can potentially change our children’s thinking and at the same the future of our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All this is set against the backdrop of our increasingly family-friendly society and national landscape.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This cannot be achieved without constant planning and Government policies that have always sought progress for everyone including our women and our daughters.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Here I would also like to laud the efforts of the men in the Malay/Muslim community who have worked together to strengthen our family institution and portray positive values and attitudes as fathers, for example, the Dads For Life movement, which has set up Dads@School to provide opportunities and space to empower fathers and learn best practices to carry out their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another initiative is the M3 BersamaMu program, led by our Assistant Kadis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It provides strong support to couples in their married life.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recognition by society can also inspire others, such as the Exemplary Father Award, organised by the Ain Society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It highlights examples of fathers in our community who are responsible and possess positive values and attitudes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our community figures such as Ustaz Mohamad Irwan Shah and Mr Sujimy Mohamed also often participate in online platforms and seminars to provide advice and lessons about family to our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These efforts demonstrate the important role that men play to portray a positive attitude in the upbringing of our children, and how women are highly regarded in our community and our faith.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us not disparage or belittle these noble efforts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our society, especially men, are not only key partners to women, but they are also advocates and companions who defend the rights of women in our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Beyond caregiving, we must also look at how to provide the best mindset and environment at home for our family members, including our children and partners to flourish and realise their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our children look at us and model our behaviours and learn from our thinking and words.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To me, patriarchal mindset and stereotypes are learned, not inherited.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recall watching an advertisement that sets out a social experiment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Groups of girls of varying age were placed in front of a camera and asked the same set of questions, "Show me how you run like a girl, how you throw like a girl, how you fight like a girl?" In the older age girls, they seem to show a weakened state, like running slowly, throwing gently or fighting softly, if there is such a term.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But in the younger girls, there was not any difference between what they demonstrated and what the other boys demonstrated; they ran just as fast, threw just as far and fought just as hard, if not faster, further or even better.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How did this phrase "like a girl" become a derogatory term?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our boys cannot think of themselves to be superior.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our girls should not feel inferior because of who they are.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can dispel this notion and support our children in our homes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As fathers, how we treat, speak and respect women in our lives would be how our daughters would expect to be treated and what is expected of our sons, as the measure of a man.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have made great progress as a nation in terms of women's development for several decades and we shall continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to act and build upon the good work and past contributions of the Government, community and social activists.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also look forward to the action plan and consolidated views in the White Paper to be presented.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope we can see further promotion of an environment that is both conducive to child caregiving and welcoming for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can do this by implementing policies that signal child caregiving as a shared responsibility between parents.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened to hear from Minister of State Sun Xueling about the theme on strengthening support on caregiving.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to sharing of parental leave that is being recommended in the joint Paper by PAP Women's Wing, I have other suggestions as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, they need to seek special approval for childcare subsidies on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, to implement a network of temporary childcare services that can be provided by pre-approved childcare centres.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this age of flexible working arrangements and working from home, such service can provide urgent and temporary respite care so that stay-at-home moms or dads can attend to urgent work or business.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I will elaborate on these suggestions and more in the full debate of the White Paper when presented.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I refer to Member's Ms He Ting Ru's reference to the Workers' Party 2020 manifesto on enhanced fertility support.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Members in this House know that I have been speaking on egg-freezing since I came into this House.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I feel that this is an important topic and, along the way, I met with some setbacks.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After all, it is not something that everyone can agree with.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am glad that there has been some progress, and this is also part of the PAP Women's Wing's recommendation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am also glad that the Workers' Party supports this position.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Over the years, I have also raised questions on IVF, PGS and requested MOH for updates on egg freezing and sperm bank.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In July 2019, the PAP Women's Wing also did a survey on journey to parenthood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: By then, I have also visited over 400 Tampines families with newborns.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I had a chat with them on their journey to parenthood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The waiting time for all three clinics has been cut considerably.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I also want to take this opportunity to thank the many families who shared their stories – some inspiring, some heartbreaking – but it helps us to understand what you are going through, so that we can speak for you and improve on it.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is heartening to see many Members speak very passionately about various aspects of women’s development.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are clearly united by our common desire to see issues facing women being addressed and for women to be truly empowered to realise their aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is indeed encouraging to see the evolution and development of efforts to empower, support and protect women over the years, through the relentless pursuit by Members of Parliament (MPs) to build on existing policies, the advocacy and community groups who continue to champion for women and the Government that is willing to listen, consider views and make changes where appropriate.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have had the opportunity to walk this journey with PPIS before I became MP, working on several papers with the PAP Women’s Wing, participating in debates as a backbencher and now, working together with Minister of State Sun Xueling and Minister of State Low Yen Ling on the Conversations on Women’s Development.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I would refer to three themes: to empower, support and protect women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We begin with the efforts to empower women to thrive at work and have equal opportunities as men.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In Parliament, Ms Tin Pei Ling had asked about the gender wage gap and often called for digital fluency among women as this could open up new career opportunities for them in the digital age.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Tin, and yourself, Mdm Deputy Speaker, and Miss Cheryl Chan had raised concerns about the representation of women in the STEM sectors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government supports the diverse career aspirations of women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We encourage women to enter occupations of their choice, including in industries that are traditionally male-dominated.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is well above the global average of 28%.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But there are still plenty of opportunities available in the technology sector, and we want more women to benefit from them and take on leadership roles.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: By entering such growth sectors, women can achieve better career and pay prospects to further close the wage gap.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One meaningful development in creating opportunities for women in the digital sector is the SG Women in Tech initiative, which IMDA launched in 2019 with community and industry partners.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The initiative enhances support for women in the technology sector and attracts more of them to the sector.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Other MPs like Miss Cheryl Chan, Mr Darryl David and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah have made suggestions over the past years on introducing customised packages to help women update their skills and facilitate their return to the workforce after marriage or childbirth.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More recently, Ms Poh Li San and Ms Yeo Wan Ling have spoken about challenges women face in caring for their families and pursuing their careers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government, working in collaboration with different agencies, has responded to such calls over the years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have continued to develop and enhance programmes to support career mobility and help ease the transition for women back into the workforce.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Workforce Singapore (WSG)'s employment facilitation programmes and services provide support to women looking to return to the workforce after a period of absence.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They can tap on personalised career coaching and various programmes to facilitate their re-entry.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In Malay):   Many programmes have been created at the national level to support and help women to continue working and achieve their aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Although some still hold stereotypes that a woman’s place is in the kitchen or at home, there are many others who want women to be given opportunities and choices.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Society and businesses have much to gain from the valuable contributions of Malay women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many young Malay women also want a different future, full of opportunities to succeed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Furthermore, having two incomes in each Malay family strengthens their financial stability.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Beyond initiatives to encourage reskilling and employment at the national level, M3 agencies also have programmes that are customised to the needs of Malay women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One example is the Back-to-Work Women programme by MENDAKI SENSE.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It prepares women to return to the workforce and connects them to employers who are hiring workers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope Malay women will always be supported in chasing their dreams.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I heard the issues raised by Ms Raeesah Khan earlier.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She mentioned the issue of female genital cutting, tudung and polygamy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Her points are similar to the recommendations seen in the Lepak Conversations report which we have also received.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have actually spoken to these activists before and I am indeed proud of these young people who want to stand up for something that they believe is important.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But they also understand the complexities of these issues within our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The issue of female genital cutting, for instance.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government does not support practices that cause harm to young women or girls.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MUIS also holds the same view and has explained that Islam does not support any procedure that harms individuals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But the fact is, there are different opinions in our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, we should resolve this matter, not by prescribing rules, but by understanding and talking or discussing with the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, this shows that ROMM’s efforts have been effective.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It was not only raised by Mr Faisal Manap, but by PAP Members of Parliament as well.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Dr Intan, Mr Zainal, our President herself raised this issue when she was in Parliament.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is something that has been discussed and will be given due attention.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should hold discussions with all levels of society, not just with the Muslim community, and this will take time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, the issues raised are certainly issues that may have been brought up.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But in order to resolve these issues properly, I think we need to fully understand and know our community to find the solutions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: And we should encourage everyone to be edified and bring them towards a paradigm shift in a judicious manner.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): For women to pursue their aspirations unencumbered, women need to be supported with their caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Men can be caregivers too and the Government also supports them in this area.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Yet, women are still the primary caregivers in most instances.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are many reasons for this, including gender bias, stereotypes and pervasive socio-cultural expectations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many women dedicate their lives to caring for their families and may thus feel compelled to give up formal employment.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To address this, the Government encourages men to share the caregiving load.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have enhanced parental leave schemes and introduced flexibility for fathers to share a portion of their wives' maternity leave.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also work with community partners such as Families for Life and the Centre for Fathering, which drives the Dads for Life movement, to promote active fatherhood.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many men are stepping up proactively and we applaud their contributions towards building more supportive and resilient families.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over the past years, Members have actively flagged the difficulties which some women caregivers experience and called for stronger support for them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2020, Ms Carrie Tan urged the Government to consider valuing the unpaid care work of women and legislating workplace policies to support working caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since 2017, Mr Louis Ng has been a strong advocate for greater support for single parents, amongst the many things he champions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Responding to the diverse challenges faced by women caregivers, the Government has made significant efforts to relieve the load they experience.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For childcare, the Government has expanded preschool places and ensured its affordability.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Regardless of their working status, all parents of Singapore Citizen children also receive basic subsidies for childcare and infant care services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For eldercare, the Government has been growing the capacity of community care services and making them more accessible to better meet the needs of our seniors and their caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Its measures cover aspects like care navigation, respite care, financial support, workplace support and caregiver empowerment and training.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To support retirement adequacy of those who had low incomes during their working years and now have less in retirement, the Government introduced the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: About two-thirds of Silver Support recipients are women, many of whom were probably caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is one of the many schemes which help to safeguard the continued financial stability and well-being of women as they age.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to grow such efforts to support women caregivers, no matter the circumstances they face.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As part of this process, we constantly review feedback from Members and the public to propose further action to support women in their caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The issue that had initially sparked off the national discussion on women's development was the concern about violence against women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At that juncture, in July 2020, the PAP Women's Wing immediately came up with a statement strongly denouncing violence against women and shared concerns about the sentencing in that case with the Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Following that, the Review of the Sentencing Framework for Sexual and Hurt Offences was conducted and, consequently, there were inter alia increase in the penalties for specific sexual offences.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We continue to face new and emerging challenges that disproportionately affect women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Technology has caused the proliferation of sexual violence in cyberspace.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many women must deal with unwanted sexual messages and calls, non-consensual sharing of intimate images, voyeurism, sexual harassment and objectification.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This has gotten worse with COVID-19 as people spend more time online.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Such behaviour negatively impacts the physical and mental well-being of victims and is unacceptable.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As with many past issues affecting women, the complex task of tackling online harms also requires solutions that extend beyond new legislation from the Government.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: During MCI's 2021 COS Debate, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann shared how the Government was collaborating with community partners interested to shape a safe cyberspace for women and girls.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have since followed up with real action.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah also made reference to this.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are fortunate to tap on the expertise of 48 members who come from across the people, public and private sectors, exemplifying the importance of a partnership approach.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As one of its co-chairs, I see the AfA as an important way to rally Singaporeans and spark more initiatives to foster a better digital culture.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must ensure that women and girls enjoy the same freedom and confidence online that they experience in real life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government's work on online harms is an example of how we are working with partners to defend the progress achieved by women amidst nascent threats.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our women have continued to break barriers and achieve new heights across various social indicators, including in literacy, employment rates and leadership in many professional domains.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our engagements have created space for all stakeholders to share their concerns frankly.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Amidst this careful and sensitive approach, Singaporean women have achieved significant progress.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government will continue to reach out to women, represent their voices and champion their progress.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of the points which Members raised today echo the Government's ongoing efforts to uplift Singaporean women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We continue in this endeavour for we are not just speaking up for women, we are speaking up for the future generation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are speaking today not because women are weak.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are speaking because men and women are strong and can change the tide of time, challenge unfairness and take action that can meaningfully change lives of future generations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The amount of feeling and the long number of speakers are indicative of how important this topic is.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We hope to see concrete steps taken to effect change, whether through legislative amendments or policy overhaul.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Be that as it may, I would again reiterate that when we decided to bring this Private Members' Motion as a party, my colleagues and I felt strongly about how the issues we raised affect both ourselves and also, the women and men in our lives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Mr Leon Perera spoke about the three women in his life – his mother, his wife and his daughter – and how he wants to see a world where women were no longer boxed into long-held stereotypes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: He shared how men and employers have key roles to play in abolishing sexist attitudes, and how we can accelerate progress by having anti-discrimination legislation while working together to teach the principles of gender equality to our children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: My Sengkang GRC colleague Mr Louis Chua shared why it is important that our care-related policies do not ironically perpetuate stereotypes and reinforce notions on gender roles.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Both men and women must not be forced to make the false choice of choosing between work or family, and we need to ensure adequate support is granted to our caregivers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: He also mentioned the important role of fathers in caring for their children – all the while leading by example as told by the number of times his little two-year-old featured in our Zoom calls while he was on papa duty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Mr Vikram Nair recounted what participants had shared at a dialogue session he attended, including their experiences of facing discrimination at the workplace during pregnancy or difficulties in re-entering the workforce after devoting several years to caregiving.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Ms Raeesah Khan spoke about sexual violence and survivor care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: She noted that we need to ensure that survivors are given adequate support to ensure that they are able to address the trauma they faced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: She also touched on three pressing issues in her community: female genital cutting, polygamy and the hijab.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah called for a whole-of-society and community mindset shift, including for boys and their caregivers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: She said that women should be the allies of each other and act in solidarity with women from marginalised groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Mr Zhulkarnian Abdul Rahim mentioned the important role of men and fathers in this conversation; and Miss Cheng Li Hui, I thank her for her views as well on egg freezing and fertility support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Mr Gerald Giam in his speech called for more openness in our immigration and visa policies for foreign spouses of Singapore Citizens to strengthen the Singapore Core, for more support to be extended to single parents and for policies to promote flexible work arrangements, all of which benefit both men and women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Ms Sylvia Lim focused on the challenge facing political parties in Singapore in finding sufficient numbers of able and willing women to step up to being parliamentary candidates and political leaders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: She noted that while Singapore had made progress, greater success was more likely if the social norms supported gender-equal choices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: She was cautiously optimistic that the element of political competition would pressure political parties to field more able women, in order to gain support from a more demanding electorate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Moreover, the most lucrative and fastest growing sectors remain male-dominated and reduced participation could be symptomatic of the difficulty that women face in breaking into such jobs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: He also proposed various measures to support women and working mothers, and to address the gender pay gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: These are just the main topics relating to the barriers to gender equality and there are many more which I have received in the form of comments and emails.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: These topics range from the concerns raised about fertility challenges that women face and women’s health in the form of the chronic management of common conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome and its associated co-morbidities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: To summarise, it is good to hear that across the aisle, we are in general agreement that gender equality has to be pushed to the forefront of national discourse.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And since it is still Olympic season, it cannot escape our attention that changes are also sweeping through sports as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It is notable that the Tokyo 2020 Olympics saw attention being given to the outfits of female Olympians, and many commented positively on the choice of the German gymnastics women’s team and Norwegian beach volleyball women’s team to wear attire that they felt most comfortable with.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It is also heartening to note that female top athletes such as Naomi Osaka and Simone Biles are the ones who are leading the way in raising issues relating to mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While it is important to make our policy positions and stand clear, we must take tangible action to effect change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This is clearly not a silver bullet, but an important next step to send a signal, to set the tone for the foundational principle of gender equality that we should put at the forefront of all our policies and laws.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: (In Mandarin):   Madam Deputy Speaker, I would like to reiterate that giving equal treatment to men and women should be a fundamental safeguard of a society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The Government should also provide more channels to report sexual harassment and abuse.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: As a responsible citizen, we must fulfil our duties towards each other.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: (In English): I started this debate by speaking about my maternal grandmother.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: She would be so happy to see how little girls today do not have to fight for a right to get themselves educated in Singapore, and no longer need to hide books to read surreptitiously.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: But she would be first to say that we must not rest on our laurels and carry on working towards a world of gender equality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And now, I would also like to close with a big note of thanks to my father.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: He was born just after the war, the last of 10 children in an extremely traditional family who viewed boys as far superior to girls.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: After my sister and I were born, my mother told me that she felt a lot of pressure to try for a third child, in the hope that they would have a boy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: When she brought this up with my father, his answer was short and sharp, "What's wrong with my daughters?" he asked.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I am incredibly grateful that my father has lived his whole life by these words, believing and supporting his daughters with his heart and soul to live our lives in accordance with our own choices – whether or not he agreed with us! – and I know that I would not be here without this commitment that he has given us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I also do not think that he, as a lifelong workaholic at the workplace, would have expected himself to become so involved in the care and nurturing of his beloved grandsons in his 70s, which has been critical in supporting me in my own journey here today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I can only hope that many more of us show our wives, mothers and daughters the same belief and love that I experienced as we move towards greater gender equality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It is not even just a women’s issue.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: We have now come to the conclusion of the debate and I shall put the question to the House for decision.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: We have an amendment proposed by Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: The amendment is that the words proposed by Mr Vikram Nair be added in line 3 after the word "society".

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: The original Motion, as amended, is now before the House.
